speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the promotion of vocational education in Canada, and to appropriate the sum of $750,000 per annum for fifteen years for such purpose, payments to be made conditional upon agreements with the respective provincial governments.

maintopic: VOCATIONAL EDUCATION
subtopic: PROPOSED ANNUAL EXPENDITURE OP $750,000 CONDITIONAL UPON AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
This is a motion dealing with what is called vocational education rather than with what has been better known in this house as technical education. I understand that in recent years a distinction has been established between the two terms, and it is now considered among educationists throughout the world that the term technical education has become associated rather with work of a scientific or investigational nature and work of university grade, while vocational education is considered a broader term, including what we formerly referred to as technical education. The new term, vocational education, I understand has been adopted pretty generally in the Department of Labour during recent years, and the publication of that department is now known as a pamphlet on vocational education. I see by newspaper reports also that in some of the provinces of Canada officers of provincial governments who formerly were known as technical education officers now are known as vocational education officers. Therefore the term "vocational" education has been adopted in this resolution instead of the term formerly used, which was "technical" education. Otherwise, the motion in its general scope proposes an annual expenditure of $750,000 for a period of fifteen years next ensuing, to aid in the great work of vocational education and vocational training throughout the Dominion of Canada.
The house will remember that as far back as the year 1919 an act was passed by this parliament providing for an expenditure of 810,000,000 at the rate of 81,000,000 per annum to assist in the work of technical education throughout Canada, in conjunction with the provincial authorities in every instance. That act ran its course and expired in the year 1929, and at that time there had been expended on technical education in Canada by this government the sum of $7,964,000, or

an average annual expenditure of $796,000 instead of the $1,000,000 which was provided by the act of 1919.
In the year 1929, therefore, it was found that there was still a substantial balance on hand of the money which parliament had appropriated to this special purpose. The balance in 1929 amounted to roughly $2,350,000, and it became a question whether the work should be continued and the original amount fully expended, or whether the work should be abandoned in that year. In 1929 this parliament passed a further act, which is chapter 8 of the statutes of 1929, making provision for further expenditure in regard to technical education in order to utilize the unspent balance of the money, and it was then provided that the unspent money might continue to be appropriated and spent among the provinces still entitled to a grant until the year 1934. At this date there is still an unexpended balance, amounting in round numbers to a million and a quarter dollars, which is available for the purpose of technical education. It is now proposed to make a new grant to apply to all the provinces upon equal terms and in proportion to their respective populations. The grant now proposed amounts to $750,000 per annum, and the period during which that grant will be paid is the next fifteen years.
The general purpose of this grant will be very largely the same as that of the grant made under the statute of 1919. There are some slight changes, it is true; these will be developed as the matter proceeds before this house. One or two of them I might mention now. In the grant made in 1919 agriculture was excluded as a matter of technical education. Under the present proposal agriculture will not be excluded, -but it will be open to the provincial governments to make such representations as they see fit to the government here in order that the grant, or parts of the grant, may be appropriated to special courses such as those provinces desire to have carried on within their respective territories. Another distinction between the present proposal and the former is that under the former proposal a limitation was placed upon the amount of this fund which might be expended by any province for school buildings, equipment and the like. The limitation in the former act was placed at 25 per cent of the amount granted; that alone could be expended on buildings and equipment. That limitation has been removed under the present proposal, and it will again rest with the provincial authorities, in consultation with the government here, to expend such part of that money as is

Vocational Education
deemed essential for the purposes of buildings and equipment. It is realized that in some provinces the work of vocational education has been carried on to a much greater extent than in other provinces. Some of them have only within recent years seriously taken up the question, and in such provinces the provision of buildings and equipment is a more serious matter than it is in some of the older provinces which for years have been engaged in this w'ork and have carried it on most successfully. There are other minor distinctions between the present proposal and the act of 1919 which will be developed as the measure proceeds through the house.
I do not think there will be more than one opinion as to the propriety of granting money for this special purpose. I had the honour a quarter of a century ago of discussing the question in this house and elaborating as fully as I was able to do the case in favour of a federal grant for technical education. I think it is realized on all hands that the technically trained man has become an essential in a country like this, and that technical education is so closely identified with the trade and commerce of the country-a matter which is entirely within the jurisdiction of this parliament-that we can well justify a grant which is going to improve our trade and commerce position or methods. And I think it is realized throughout the trading world today that technically trained men are necessary not only for production purposes in the various branches of production, but that they are just as necessary in regard to the salesmanship of the various goods produced, I remember last autumn speaking to a large manufacturer from Sheffield, a producer of cutlery goods, and he said, "We find that not only do we need highly trained men in the production of our goods, but that we need just as highly trained men in the salesmanship of our goods." So in both these instances Canada will require the same training, and the grant is made for the purpose of encouraging education along that line.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that at this stage I can usefully add anything to the remarks which I have now made. I have outlined the broad proposal contained in the resolution, and when the resolution comes to the committee stage I shall be able to give full information as desired.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Leader of the Opposition):	Mr. Speaker,
I rise not to take exception to the object of the resolution, nor indeed have I any exception to take to the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). This parliament has already by its enactments given ample evidence of its belief in technical education, and in the power of the federal government to give assistance to the provinces in furthering the work of technical or vocational education. So that with respect to the object or purpose of the resolution and the powers of this parliament, I should like it to be distinctly understood that I have no exception whatever to take. I do feel, however, that this is a moment when it would seem advisable to consider the soundness of the principle of making parliamentary grants from the federal treasury to the provinces in a manner or to an extent different from that which was contemplated in the financial arrangements made at the time of confederation and the various revisions of those arrangements which have since been made. That is the point to which I wish to speak at this time, because it seems to me to have an immediate bearing upon this resolution, and will also have a bearing upon other resolutions which will be introduced, I presume in the course of the present session, by hon. gentlemen opposite.
Confederation, as the house well knows, was effected as the result of a compromise made more particularly with respect to financial matters. When the original provinces were considering the various resolutions at the Quebec conference it became apparent that different views were entertained as to the rights which the provinces and the Dominion respectively should have in the matter of raising the necessary revenues. The provinces theretofore had had the right of raising revenues by indirect taxation; they had their own customs tariffs. It wag obvious that confederation could not be effected if the provinces were to continue to have tariffs of their own. An alternative suggestion was that this central government-the federal government- when it came into existence should raise all revenues and distribute a portion to the provinces. To that, obviously, there were certain objections. A third proposal was that the provinces should raise all of their taxation by direct methods, though the Dominion should have the right of raising taxation according to any method that in the wisdom of its own parliament seemed best. The provinces would not hear of coming into confederation on the understanding that they must raise all of their revenues by direct taxation, so the compromise effected was this-that such revenues as they did raise would be raised by direct taxation, but that the federal government out of its revenues would make annual contributions in the nature of subsidies to the provinces to
Vocational Education

make good what they might be presumed to be sacrificing in giving up their rights to raise any taxation by indirect methods. The subsidies which were agreed to at that time w&re agreed to as being of a character which would equalize the financial arrangements as between the different provinces of Canada and the Dominion. They were worked out on a per capita basis. That is the fundamental basis on which the financial arrangements between the Dominion and the provinces were made at the time and have existed ever since. As the years have gone by it has been observed that, as agreed upon originally, the subsidies were inadequate, and revisions have been made, but they have always been made with a view to effecting final and equitable arrangements as between the Dominion and the provinces so far as financial considerations are concerned.
If that method is continued I see no danger of conflict, over matters of jurisdiction, over questions of raising the necessary revenues or matters of taxation, but if it is to be departed from, if a new custom is to be permitted to grow up whereby this federal parliament is to make grants to the different provinces for all kinds of purposes, grants which are conditional upon agreement with the provinces, grants conditional upon the provinces undertaking work which possibly many of them would hesitate to undertake but for the financial aid being granted, I submit we will soon coma into a very serious situation in the relations between the Dominion and the provinces with respect to finances. For that reason, I feel that at this time the ministry might well take into consideration the wisdom of proceeding very slowly in countenancing a custom which, as I am frank to admit, has already grown up but which if continued will, I believe, give rise to serious complications.
The best brief treatise I have seen on the financial arrangements between the provinces and the Dominion is one which was published as McGill University Economic Studies No. 12, by Mr. A. W. Boos, M.A. This treatise was published by the university under the title of The Financial Arrangements Between the Provinces and the Dominion. The writer sums up in a paragraph or two the essence of what I have up to' the moment been endeavouring to say. On page 13 appears the following:
It was provided that the grants authorized by the act were to be "in full settlement of all future demands on Canada." With the exception of the possibility of a limited increase in the per capita grant, owing to an increase in population, for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, these financial arrangements might be said to be inflexible and non-adapt-
able to changing conditions. There were several reasons for this. On the one hand, the fathers of confederation thought that they had made adequate provision for provincial expenditures and, on the other hand, they thought that by placing an obstacle in the way of additional or increased grants, they would effectively cheek provincial extravagance and that the local government would be compelled to control their expenses. "And it must be observed," declared Sir Alexander Galt, in the debates on confederation in the province of Canada in 1865, "that the agreement does not contemplate any future extension of this amount. It is hoped that being in itself fixed and permanent in its character, the local government will see the importance-I may say the necessity-of their exercising a rigid and proper control over their expenditures."
And then:
In this respect, a quotation from one of the Hon. George Brown's speeches delivered in the year 1867, is especially significant. "Let this, too," he declared, "ever be kept in mind, that the $2,630,000 to be distributed to the local government from the federal chest is to be in full and final extinguishment of all claims hereafter for local purposes, and if this from any cause does not suffice, the local government must supply all deficiencies from direct taxes on their own localities."
And in conclusion:
The financial arrangements were thought to be final and complete: they were consummated in an environment of concession and compromise, in a spirit of fairness, and with a sense of equity.
I believe that the soundness of the position taken at the time of confederation by those who had to do with the framing of the act must be wholly apparent. The argument which was urged most strongly with respect to not making contributions from the federal treasury to the provinces was that any course of that kind would render the executives of the provinces independent to a considerable extent of their legislatures, and, moreover, that- it would prevent the effective control of public expenditures being exercised by the government which was responsible for making the grant. In other words, a practice of that kind was viewed as being contrary to what is essential under any system of responsible self-government. I think that must be wholly apparent. If the executives of the different provinces are granted considerable sums of money from the federal government they are in this manner placed in possession of amounts of money which they are at liberty to spend without reference to the legislatures themselves; it may be that the object upon which the money is to be spent may be named, but the executives are at liberty to expend it without encountering the necessity of raising a corresponding amount in taxation in order to have the required revenue. They are put

Vocational Education
in the position where they, as executives, are rendered wholly independent of the legislatures from which, as executives, they derive their authority. In the old days when revenues in part were derived from territorial and casual sources the executive was in .that position. It was free to ignore its following in the legislative assembly because its revenues came from sources other than taxation. Responsible government put an end to that kind of thing because it necessitated that revenues should be raised through taxation and that the executive'should be responsible to the legislature with respect to all moneys so raised.
If the amounts contributed as grants were small and incidental the question might not come to assume the proportions it is now assuming, but there has grown up in this country a practice entirely different from anything contemplated at the time the original financial arrangements were made or at the time of any subsequent revision, a practice which seems to me to be most unsound.
The present resolution places in the possession of the provincial governments a sum of $/50,000 annually for a period of fifteen years, amounting in all to something like SI 1,250,000. With respect to that $11,250,000 the executives of the provinces will not have to consider their followers; they will have the money handed to them and quite independently of the legislatures they will be free to deal with it. I submit that the effect of that will be simply that the executives undoubtedly will apply this money for the purpose for which it has been granted, but they will take money which otherwise would have been required and raised for the purposes of technical or vocational education and apply it to some other kind of service which they may find it desirable to initiate. In the way of technical or vocational education there will be neither more nor less than there otherwise would have been. That means that the provincial governments will get into the habit of extravagance; it means that they will not be obliged to control their revenues as they otherwise would, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that surely this is the time, of all times, when with respect to municipalities, provincial governments and the federal government there is need for the utmost scrutiny of expenditures and for economy wherever that can be possibly brought about. To render an executive independent of a legislature, to however small a degree, is a step backward; it is a step in the wrong direction and it is a step which should not
be countenanced by this parliament. In addition, a step which will render a provincial legislature more extravagant with its expenditures than it would otherwise be, is not one which should be encouraged by this house.
I know the late Liberal administration was criticized on the floor of the house and throughout the country for having permitted some of these grants from the dominion to the provinces to expire when the statutory term was reached and for not having renewed them. May I say that the reason the late government took that course was not through any lack of sympathy with respect to the various purposes for which these moneys were voted. It was solely due to the necessity which the government saw, in view of the great obligations which had come upon the federal government as a result of the war, of exercising all the economy possible in the matter of public expenditures and of seeing to it that where great sums of taxation had to be raised to meet entirely new obligations, those sums should be devoted to federal purposes first. In other words, we found, as the present administration I am sure is also finding in its case, that the revenues at the time we came into office were not sufficient to meet the expenditures. There was a great national debt. The country was going deeper and deeper into debt. The right hon. Mr. Fielding, at the time minister of finance, took very strongly the view that unless we could balance the national budget the credit of Canada would continue to suffer from year to year; that the first duty of the administration of the day was to seek to balance the budget; and that having balanced the budget, its next duty was as far as possible to reduce taxation. We felt that unless we kept down debt and taxation, we could not hope to improve the financial position of the dominion. The present administration is now faced with a similar situation. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) brings down his budget, we shall hear how much the public debt of the country has increased. We shall probably learn that there is a deficit running up into the vicinity of $100,000,000 for the last fiscal year. If that be the case, is it not reasonable to ask the administration to consider whether this is the time that it should begin to extend to the provinces grants for the purpose of carrying on work which is avowedly theirs, or whether it should not first consider the methods that will best serve to reduce debt and taxation.
To make quite clear the point that I have in mind, may I ask this question:	Why
should the provinces with respect to par-
Vocational Education

ticular services be dealt with in a manner different from that which governs with respect to any other services which under the constitution they may have to perform? Take for example the administration of justice. Under the British North America Act this parliament appoints and provides for the payment of the salaries of judges. It does not prbvide for the administration of justice apart from the payment of salaries of judges. The administration of justice is essential; it is something which all will regard as highly necessary. Why should the dominion not vote certain sums of money to the provinces to assist them in the administration of justice? Why limit financial grants to technical education? Why limit them to highways? Why limit them to old -age pensions, agricultural instruction, housing or other specially selected services, essential as they may be? If the principle is a sound one, its application should not be limited at all. My contention is that it is unsound to adopt, with respect to any services which are imposed by the British North America Act upon the provinces, a principle that cannot be universally applied.
May I say further in support of the view I am seeking to present, that I am not aware of the provinces making any contribution towards the increased obligations which the federal treasury is ealled upon to meet, and, with the passing of the years, the obligations of the federal treasury have increased many times over those of the provinces themselves. The federal government assumed practically the whole obligation with respect to the great war. It assumed the obligation of the cost of the war, and practically all of the obligations that have arisen out of the war. It assumed the complete burden of pensions, and we know how vast in their total amount pensions are becoming. The men who are receiving the pensions are citizens of the provinces as well as of the dominion, but the provinces are in no way contributing towards the extra obligation which the dominion has, and to-day federally we are going deeper and deeper in debt. If our national debt and our taxes are increasing, this is because of the extra federal burden which the federal government is assuming but which the provinces do not share in at all. In these circumstances it seems to me that the anly wise and sound course to be followed financially is that each party should meet the services it is expected to meet and not go beyond them without some revision of the entire financial arrangements. For example, in regard to the obligations on the part of the federal government in one matter only, a

return was called for a day or two ago by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) with respect to pensions. In the return the following figures appear:

This is roughly $60,000,000 of an annual pension list, the greater part of which did not exist when the first departure was made from the old practice of making no financial grants to the provinces other than by the subsidies that were arranged as a result of conferences between the dominion and the provinces. If the financial arrangements between the dominion and the provinces are not what they should be; if they are unjust; if they bear unfairly upon the provinces or upon the dominion, .they should be revised and care should be taken to see that the revision is just in all particulars. But I do not think it is right that without such a revision, parliament should, little by little, depart from what was the pact of confederation and assume all kinds of burdens which it is not in a position to meet and which are resulting at the present, of all times, in greater extravagance federally, provincially and municipally.
May I give one other quotation from the writer whom I have quoted? This is one that he makes from Mr. Dunkin, who participated in the debates at the time of confederation. The quotation shows very clearly that the fathers of confederation were in no doubt at all where the practice would lead if once there was to be a departure from that laid down by them as the one that should govern in financial matters between the Dominion and the provinces. At page 9, Mr. Boos says:
In the course of the debates on confederation in the parliament of the province of Canada, Mr. Dunkin, in opposing the subsidy principle, declared: "I am afraid the provincial constituencies, legislatures, and executives will all show a most calf-like appetite for the milking of this one most magnificent government cow" .... "With one accord the provincial governments will, in a quiet way, want money, and the provincial legislatures and people will want it more; grants for roads, for bridges, for schools, for charities, for contingencies of the legislature-for all manner and ends they will be wanting money, and where is it to come

Vocational Education
from? Whether the constitution of the provincial executive savours of responsible government or not, be sure it will not be anxious to place itself more under.the control of the legislature, or to make itself more odious than it can help, and the easiest way for it to get money will be from the general government/'
The writer goes on to say:
The poignancy of these remarks is revealed to a remarkable _ extent by subsequent developments and the vicissitudes of the subsidy question during the next sixty years lends a great deal of accuracy to these prognostications.
I do not think I need to stress further the point of the number of services the provinces will wish to have aided or financed by the Dominion. I should like, however, to emphasize where the practice is leading in other directions that in- other ways are inimical to our public life.
In the first place, if the practice is to be encouraged of the Dominion making special grants to the provinces for different purposes, to that extent the federal government is going to be put in a position to bring pressure to bear upon the various provinces with respect to the several matters with which they are to deal. That is not a course that should be countenanced. At the last Dominion-provincial conference, if I am not wholly mistaken, the provincial premiers were virtually unanimous in their view that such moneys as were to come to them from the federal treasury should be in the form of subsidies which each province would be free to deal with as its own requirements seemed to warrant. They were opposed to these special grants for special purposes. They wanted all the money they could get, but they wanted to be free to deal with their different requirements as they arose with an absolutely free hand, and not to be bound by any direction from a federal source.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has referred to two or three changes in the present measure from the act which previously passed this house. Those changes help to illustrate the very thing I have in mind. In the first place, my hon. friend says that in this bill provision is made that a province may use for agricultural instruction purposes moneys voted under this resolution for vocational education; in other words, the grant can be switched from one purpose to another. Now the switching of appropriations is another violation of a fundamental principle.

It may be capable in a broad sense of that interpretation. I will go that far: I am not trying to score any point; I am simply trying to bring out the truth. When parliament previously voted money for technical education, it was found that one province in particular, possibly more than one, but one certainly, the province of Prince Edward Island, I remember, did not wish to start any technical education system at all. That province contended that it was largely an agricultural province, not a manufacturing province, and it did not wish to enter upon a technical education system. Representations were made to the federal government by the province that inasmuch as they had not drawn any money from the federal grant for technical educational purposes, they should be given permission to draw an equivalent amount for agricultural instruction. That request was met, and some of the moneys previously voted for technical education went to the province of Prince Edward Island for purposes of agricultural instruction. But agriculture is something that comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces as well as under the jurisdiction of the dominion, and I submit that it is not a wise thing to begin to have appropriations for agriculture made in this parliament for the work of agriculture as it is to be carried on federally, and, as well, moneys voted in this parliament to give to the provinces to help them in their agricultural work by supplementing their own appropriations for agriculture. It results in confusion, and wherever there is confusion with respect to financial matters there generally comes to be a considerable amount of waste as well. In other words, the making of money grants is practically paying the provinces to relinquish part of their autonomy; that is what it comes to, where grants are made from the federal treasury to the provinces under agreement or with any string attached to them.
But in addition to that, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the practice is almost certain to give rise to a very serious problem in our political life, and that is the inducement it affords to a government in office or to a party seeking office to win the support of the electorate of provinces through promises which they may

May I say
this, to make quite clear what I have in mind? Had the administration which was in office at the time pursued a like course, and it might have pursued it in a way much more effective than the way taken by hon. gentlemen opposite, there is no question as to where the former administration would be in the matter of power to-day. If before the general election the Liberal government which was in office had placed in the estimates which it brought down in this house the sum of $20,000,000 for unemployment relief, to mention nothing else, I venture to say we would have heard very little of the unemployment problem in the last election; but because the government of the day sought to protect the federal treasury with respect to what it conceived to be the obligations of the federal treasury, and took a position which was essential with respect to public expenditures at a time of great obligation and great need, we suffered politically in contrast with the methods adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite. But if we had gone a step farther and had said, we are prepared to give one hundred per cent of the old age pensions, we are prepared to construct a federal highway either through aid to the provinces or by the Dominion itself, we are prepared to aid technical education and agricultural instruction in the same way as it was done before, and if we had put estimates before parliament for that purpose and voted them with the power that we had while in office, I venture to say that there could be no two points of view as to what the outcome of the election would have been. It is a very serious thing, Mr. Speaker, if in our country a course is to be embarked upon which at all subsequent elections is going to lead to

competition between the various political parties in their appeals to the electorates of the several provinces as to which is going to be most generous with public money. That I say is a very serious thing. It is easy to make promises. Hon. gentlemen opposite are going to find out how easy it is to fulfil them. But it should not be possible for any government or political party to be able to promise if returned to power to use federal moneys for provincial purposes. The constitution itself should make that impossible and such I believe was the intention. The fact that this kind of thing has happened is the strongest reason why we should now consider, at an early stage, at this second session of the new parliament, whether such a practice should be permitted to grow up in our country. I make that statement with great seriousness. My hon. friend stated that he was interested in this matter a quarter of a century ago. I can scarcely believe that at a time so long ago I had the privilege of being associated with him in connection with this very subject of technical education. A quarter of a century is a considerable portion of a man's life. Looking forward to what may happen within the next quarter of a century, I hope that before we get much farther advanced this parliament, for the country's sake, will find it possible to stop possible competition between political parties as to the use of federal funds for provincial purposes in appeals to the electorates of the provinces. When a grave danger exists it had better be frankly faced. I believe the fathers of confederation perceived the possibility when they made the very wise provision for dividing the duties and functions of governments between the dominion and the provinces and laid down the rule that the authority which expended the taxes should be the one to raise the required revenues. May I point out how fundamentally unsound is any other principle? The body which has to do with the raising of revenue should be the only one to have to do with the spending of it. A thoroughly unsound principle lies at the heart of the proposal now before the house. The proposal is that the federal government which has had and will have to raise the taxes shall transfer to the provinces the moneys received and the provinces will be free to spend such moneys without giving any account to the federal government beyond the assurance that they have received the moneys and are using them for the particular purpose prescribed. The adequate control of public expenditures in this parliament goes

Vocational Education
farther than the voting of moneys by parliament and their transfer to a legislature allowing the legislature to deal as it pleases with the money. The control of public expenditures, rightly understood, necessitates following to the last stage in expenditure the manner in which public money is expended. This legislation is a denial of that principle. At the special session of parliament a similar right and duty was denied this parliament with respect to the measure concerning unemployment relief. The government said, "When we pay the money to the provinces and the payment is acknowledged by them, our responsibility ends." Hon. members on this side of the house took the position that the Auditor General of this country should audit in detail every dollar of expenditure appropriated by this parliament. If once we get away from that principle not only in regard to hundreds and thousands, but m regard to millions of dollars, where shall we have any sound basis for the control of public expenditures in relation to the financing of the country?
To give hon. members an idea of the proportions these grants are assuming I will quote to parliament what was paid out of the federal treasury to the provinces during the time the late Liberal administration was in office. On occasions the electors have been told that the late administration was heartless, that we made no payments to the provinces and that we were depriving them of all funds from the federal treasury. While in office we carried out the provisions of the statutes we found on the books when we assumed office and made payments in accordance with those provisions. I have the figures before me showing the grants for the fiscal years ranging from 1921-22 to 1929-30. Here is the statement in tabulated form:

From the table it will be seen that in a period of eight years, not quite the whole period of time we were in office, the grants made to the provinces in subsidies by the Liberal administration amounted to $99,334,132. Special subsidies to the maritime provinces amounted to $4,800,000, or a total paid out in subsidies of $104,134,132. The grant for highways was $16,065,990; for agricultural instruction, $1,993,482; for technical education, $6,890,375; for amortization of debt against certain school buildings, $133,389; for unemployment offices, $1,337,032; for eradication of venereal diseases, $1,000,353; lor old age pensions, $3,770,991; for unemployment relief paid out by the Labour department, $1,004,874; making a total grant for these services of $32,198,486. In connection with unemployment relief the amount of $3,858,184 was paid out by the Department of Pensions and National Health. The total payment for war pensions was $233,804,397, the two last-named items making a total of $237,662,581. It was estimated that the grants for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1931, for the purposes I have mentioned would be $71,931,229. If that estimate is nearly accurate it would appear that in the time within the 9 years during' which the late administration held office S445,924,428 was paid out of the federal treasury to the provinces. If we take an average of the figures I have quoted to ascertain expenditure over a ten year period, we find that within the past decade there was an expenditure of over half a billion dollars from the federal treasury to the different provinces. Certainly such expenditures were never contemplated at the time of confederation when the subsidies were fixed at a definite amount nor were grants to that extent contemplated when subsequent revisions were made.

May I add that in addition to all these grants the provinces in other respects have been dealt with in an exceptionally liberal manner by the federal government. During the time the late administration was in office the maritime provinces had their grievances, reviewed by the Duncan commission, and as a result adjustments were made which have resulted in additional payments to the maritime provinces in special subsidies alone of $4,800,000. There have been for provincial purposes many additional payments. The prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have had their natural resources returned to them. In addition to that this parliament has generously continued to those provinces the subsidies which they had been receiving in lieu of their resources. They have received back what was left of their resources, and the subsidies which originally were given in lieu of resources have been continued. In the province of British Columbia the government gave back the Peace River block, the railway belt lands, to which the province had no legal claim and in addition continued to the province of British Columbia the subsidy that province was receiving during the period this government had control of those particular lands. The position taken by the late administration concerning the water powers in the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec was that these powers would by agreement between the dominion and the provinces be treated as though they belonged to the provinces although the matter had not been finally judicially decided. The correspondence reveals that as a matter of public policy we were quite prepared to concede to the province of Ontario with respect to water power on the St. Lawrence exactly the same rights as the province of Quebec asserted were her rights with respect to such water power. I may say that continuously the federal parliament has treated the provinces most liberally with respect to all natural resources, giving them additional sources of revenue, and the like. On the other hand, the federal government has received from the provinces nothing in exchange voluntarily or otherwise. The time I think has arrived when this matter should be made the subject of a conference concerned with a financial readjustment between the dominion and the provinces. If it does appear that the provinces are entitled to something more than the subsidies as fixed at the present time, by all means let the subsidies be revised and an increased amount given. A step which might serve the purpose equally well, and possibly even better, would be for this federal government to take over some of the sendees which at present 
are being left to the provinces. Whether this should be done in addition to payment of subsidies, or in exchange, in whole or in part, for subsidies to which the provinces are entitled, would be a matter for negotiation. If, for example, the intention of the administration opposite is to meet one hundred per cent of the cost of old age pensions apart from administration. I submit it would be entirely wrong for this parliament to vote all the money required to pay old age pensions and leave it to the different provinces to administer the vast sums thus appropriated. If one hundred per cent is to be paid, by all means let the appropriations made by this parliament be administered by the government which is responsible for voting the money, and let every cent of the expenditure be checked up by the Auditor General, who is responsible to this parliament and removeable only by an address of both houses of parliament. Any other basis would be altogether unsound. I know that the late Liberal administration did assume half the obligation with respect to old age pensions, and to that extent our action at the time did not conform to what at the moment I am putting forward as the right course to be pursued, but that step was taken at the time because of certain constitutional difficulties believed to exist with respect to the federal government administering an old age pension scheme. If those difficulties still exist they should be removed, before the appropriations are increased. I do submit that fundamentally, with respect to the finances of the country, this parliament should adhere to the essential view that the body which raises the money must be the body which will have the responsibility for expending it and vice versa, and that the responsibility must be exercised in the light of a full and complete audit by the officer appointed by this parliament for that purpose.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just this word in conclusion: The Prime Minister is filling the important portfolio of Minister of Finance, and has given, as we all know, very careful thought and study to many of these financial problems. He has addressed this house on different occasions with respect to what in his view was the position that should be taken by this parliament in financial matters, and he has stressed, as the leader of any political party or any government must stress, the necessity for economy in public expenditures and above all the necessity for a nation, having regard to its credit, not to go deeper and deeper into debt but to seek to balance its budget. May I say that if the budget of this parliament were balanced and taxation were down to a

Vocational Education
moderate level, perhaps I would feel a little less concerned about being over-generous with the provinces in the way of contributing a portion of our revenues to them for provincial purposes. But when we know the public debt of the country to be what it is to-day, when we know it is going to be increased this very year by something like $100,000,000, then I say this is a time we should begin not to look around to see w'here we can spend more money, but where we can successfully economize in public expenditures.
The Prime Minister, as leader of the opposition in this house on March 18, 1928, spoke as follows:
I say that we should place upon the statute books of this country at the earliest possible moment a provision by which a sinking fund will be set up such as they have in Great Britain and in other countries, so that we shall be enabled, within a period to be mentioned, absolutely to wipe out and eliminate the national debt of Canada.
I assume that when the Prime Minister brings down his budget we will find therein some provision in the nature of a sinking fund. If that provision is made, the object will be to wipe out and eliminate the national debt of Canada. I ask my hon. friends who are members of the administration, are you helping in that direction when you ask this parliament, at this of all times, to increase its expenditure by making this contribution in the nature of an additional grant to the provinces for vocational education? Will you be assisting the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister in his great objective when other demands of a similar kind will be made later on? What is the next sentence:
What is the province of Ontario doing?
This is interesting:
What is the province of Ontario doing? Do hon. gentlemen realize that in Ontario they have provided for the setting aside, of $3,000,000 every year so that at the end of forty years their debt wall be entirely wiped out, half being provided by public utilities, and the other half from the taxpayers of the province itself? Do hon. gentlemen realize that?
Those were the words of the Prime Minister, speaking two years ago from where 1 am speaking now. May I ask the house, using his words:	Do hon. members realize
that while the province of Ontario has made provision for wiping out its debt in forty years, by a sinking fund which sets aside $3,000,000 a year, we in this federal parliament are voting in appropriations to the province of Ontario on one account or another a sum, not of $3,000,000 a year but of over $4,000,000 a year to be paid from the federal treasury out of the taxes of the 22110-1251
people? Do hon. members realize that? Let us see what was voted to the province of Ontario over a period of eight years, when the late Liberal administration was in office. The figures are as follows:

That is an average of just about $4,000,000 a year. That is the amount that goes out of this federal treasury to the province of Ontario, leaving that province free to spend it with respect to the different services named or, as regards the subsidies, as the province wishes, and the province on its part is- setting aside not $4,000,000 a year, the amount it receives from us, but $3,000,000 a year, as a sum sufficient to wipe out its entire pubiic debt in that time. When Canada has a debt such as exists at the present time in this Dominion, a debt of over two billions of dollars, why should this parliament pay off the debts of the provinces before it begins to pay off its own public debt? I submit that at this time, when we are seeking to raise the revenues necessary to meet current expenditures, and find this impossibie and have to resort to the extremes in taxation to which we have already gone, and may yet have to go, we had better begin to pay off our own debt first and then, when that is done, there will be time to consider what is advisable as regards being more generous to the provinces. Let us be just before we are generous. Following what I have read, the Prime Minister said:
Suppose we seek to retire only $1,500,000,000 of this debt by a statutory sinking fund, by means of a provision placed upon the statute books of this country, so that the demands and pressure by political supporters would not induce the finance minister to part with public moneys because he would have to meet these sinking fund payments. It would ensure economy in the public service, and what is more, it would make the people of this country increasingly proud as they saw what President Coolidge has described as this greatest menace to our economic development, this great load of debt hanging over our necks, being gradually retired.
There is an interesting phrase used by the Prime Minister in that paragraph:
.... the demands and pressure by political supporters would not induce the finance minister to part with public moneys because he would have to meet these sinking fund payments.

What is this resolution other than the result of the pressure which is being put on the finance minister for political reasons, and no others, pressure mostly of his own creation? Now, I should like to read two paragraphs more of what the Prime Minister said:
Is this country to continue to be menaced by this economic evil, by this debt hanging over our heads? Are we to continue, of all countries in the world, to make no provision for the future? Are we to be content to expend our patrimony day by day, without putting anything aside to take care of the long days of the future that are before us? I say it is unfair to ourselves, it is unfair to the taxpayers of this country to extract from them each year these increasingly large sums of money and make no provision for the retirement of our national obligations.
A little further on he says:
It has been said that no government is ever defeated because it is extravagant. That well may be. It well may be that the people may be debauched with their own revenues, and be taught that all you have to do is to spend their taxes freely among them and then you have succeeded, but what is the effect upon the life of the nation as a nation?
I commend that last paragraph to the Prime Minister and the members of his administration. The Prime Minister says: You may retain power by debauching the nation with its own revenues, but he also asks what is going to become of the nation in the long run?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to my hon, friend1-and I do so with all respect and sincerity-that he consider how far he should press this resolution at this time in the light of the financial situation of this country as he and his colleagues know it to be. Why fix a term of fifteen years as the period over which this sum of money should continue to be paid? I do not see why we should bind subsequent parliaments and possibly administrations to payments of this kind running on for fifteen years, that is until 1946. The time surely ought to be shorter than that. May I say this? Frequently of late we have heard mention of the Dominiomprovincial conference that is soon to be held. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he consider the wisdom of limiting the period of time for which this amount is to be paid to the period that may intervene between the present and the holding of that conference. Or, as an alternative, the withholding of the measure altogether- which would be preferable-until after the Dominion-provincial conference and until after there has been opportunity for careful discussion there of this whole matter. I know my hon. friend is seeking to fulfil an obligation. He has made promises that something of this kind will be dong, and being a fMr. Mackenzie King.]
man of his word, he is seeking to fulfil those promises; but I believe the public at large will credit him with an even finer sincerity if in view of the situation as it is in Canada today, he declines to proceed further with this resolution or the bill based upon it until the provinces and the Dominion in conference have jointly considered what should be done with respect to the financial arrangements between them.

Mr. Speaker, so frequently from this quarter we are obliged to offer adverse criticism that I am very glad indeed to-day to be able to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) on the admirable statement -which he has given to the house, and I shall be very glad indeed to support the resolution.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), it seems to me, has been attempting to magnify a molehill into a mountain. He tells us that this year we shall probably be $100,000,000 behind. If we are so far behind in our budget, it is well for us to remember that all the expenditure called for by this resolution is three quarters of a million dollars -considerably less than 1 per cent of the deficit that the leader of the opposition believes we shall have to face this year.
I am afraid that if I were in a facetious mood I would have to begin by rather objecting to the resolution on the ground that "it is contrary to the terms of the British North America Act". Really I would commend the Minister of Justice for the skilful way in which he has avoided the British North America Act. I would suggest to the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) that if she could simply show that peace was in some way connected with trade and commerce, that it tended to promote trade and commerce, she would not have the slightest difficulty about being able to secure a grant for her professorships and scholarships from the present government, notwithstanding the British North America Act.
The leader of the opposition was rather captious in his criticism, when he went so far as to criticise the changes which have been made in the proposed resolution as compared with the terms of the old act. I take it that these changes indicated by the minister represent the lessons which have been learned during the past years. It is surely perfectly legitimate that the great vocation of agriculture should be placed on the same basis as other vocations. There seems no reason why that should not be done. In fact, now that agriculture has developed so many tech-

Vocational Education
nical features it is eminently in keeping with general developments that this should be the case. Further than that, the other change mentioned, that of permitting the provinces to decide just what percentage of the grant should go into equipment and what into actual teaching, appears to me to be a reasonable one; the provinces ought to be allowed some discretionary power in that regard, especially when we consider, as the minister has said, that their development is at different stages.
The leader of the opposition had a good deal to say about the heavy financial burdens that this country had undertaken, and to offer that as an excuse why his government-the late government-had not continued the grants to technical education. He urged that there ought to be a balanced budget, and then that we ought to have reduced taxation and reduced debt. It is quite true, as he said, that we have a huge annual pension list of 860,000,000, but I would point out to the house that the greater part of that $60,000,000 has not been contracted because of any peaceful expenditures, but because of war, and hence this argument ought not to be used when we are discussing a matter that relates to the civil life of the country.
The leader of the opposition brought forward a number of technical objections, and as I listened to him I could well imagine myself back fifty years in the age of Gladstone with his "retrenchment and reform", because on these matters I do not believe the right hon. gentleman has travelled much in his thinking beyond the age of Gladstone and the ancient Liberals of that day. But the times have moved on. And that, may I sa3r, is the trouble with the Liberal party in Great Britain-and apparently it is going to be the trouble with the Liberal party in this country. They are refusing to recognize the changed conditions, and they satisfy themselves by mumbling old slogans at a time when they will not work.

Of course, he did mention those subsides, but this is an
example of what he would regard as a "vicious principle". Yet confederation itself was founded on what he would term the vicious principle of the collection of moneys by the federal authorities and the turning-over of those moneys to the provinces. Further, it has been a sound and well-recognized principle in British finance that certain higher authorities would give "grants in aid" to other organizations, and it has been lauded as a very satisfactory arrangement. We have had provincial grants in aid of municipalities, we have had provincial grants in aid of school boards. In short, grants in aid have become a commonplace, and in carrying out this idea of the federal government giving grants in aid of vocational education, we are but carrying out an arrangement that has frequently been practised by the British government, and by the federal government ever since confederation.
I should like to direct attention to some other ways in which we have given grants in aid. For example, we have given aid to the Canadian National Railways. I know there are dangers connected with that proceeding, but the Canadian National Railways have not been in a position to raise their own revenue. This house has raised the revenue required and we have turned over the actual expenditure of the moneys and have exercised very little control.

In spite of what
the Auditor General did, my point still stands. The fact is that as far as Canada was concerned we were not primarily responsible for the conduct of the war or for the way in which it was carried out, as we should have been if the reasoning of the hon. leader of the opposition were followed out.
It is all very well to have a readjustment of taxation as between the dominion and the provinces and I am in hearty sympathy with the leader of the opposition when he says that there should be a conference called for that purpose. That is long overdue. Undoubtedly the relationship in this regard between the dominion and the provinces is very unsatisfactory, but I would like to point out that in addition to that we have to consider other matters such as redistribution of powers as between the dominion and the provinces. It is not right simply to select one out of a number of matters and concentrate attention upon it to the exclusion of all the others. The consideration of who is responsible for unemployment should go along with the problem of who is to pay for unemployment insurance. Because of the development which has occurred in the industrial sphere it is next to impossible under modern conditions for the provinces to handle a matter of this kind.

Further there is a definite trend in the development of the industrial, commercial and financial life of this and all other countries which we ought to recognize. We live in an era of concentration. We know that we cannot have a bank limited to the provinces- that was recognized even at the time of confederation-we must have institutions which are Dominion-wnde. As a matter of fact they cannot be limited even to the dominion, they must establish relations between this and other countries. So to-day we are moving in the direction of an international bank. That illustration from the financial field is indicative of the movement going on the world over- a movement of organization and concentration. In the face of a movement of that kind it seems to me to be absolutely futile to suggest that we can revert to the conditions which existed fifty years ago or decentralize in our governmental policies and expenditures. I do not believe it can be done; we shall have to find some other solution than that.
The leader of the opposition suggests certain political dangers which may be met should this policy be persisted in. He suggests political pressure from the provinces, or by the public at the time of elections. He went so far as to say that had his government suggested the grant of 320,000,000 for unemployment relief they might still have been in power. That may be true, but I would have thought that instead of attacking the present government he would have considered that by this time he ought to have learned his lesson. After all, those in authority cannot altogether disregard popular demands. What is a government for? Surely it is to carry out the will of the people. We cannot as a house, or those who are in charge of the government cannot as a government, hold themselves aloof from the needs and the desires of the people.
It is all very well for the leader of the opposition to talk about the necessity of economizing. We all believe in economy; it is a good thing under certain circumstances but one can withhold "more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty." There is danger that we may withhold to-day the money which we ought to spend. Whatever our theories of government may be, governments to-day must assume a larger measure of responsibility for social expenditures all along the line. Nearly all governments have been forced to accept that position, and the government of Canada cannot be different in that regard from the other governments of the world.

speechtext:
I am not discussing the policy of Australia, but I would say with regard to the Australian policy:	If it is
*a fight between the moneyed interests including the Bank of England interests and the welfare of the people of Australia, the people of Australia come first. The situation we have to face in this country is somewhat similar and it is a serious one.' We have, I believe, sufficient resources:	It is a case of
utilizing these to meet national needs. How do they raise their revenue in Great Britain- income tax. Have we done much along that line? We have just a light income tax now long years after the war. We should have raised our war expenditures as we went
along, but we refused to adopt that method of financing. Had we done so we should not have had any debt now, our policy differed from that in Great Britain in that during the war we refused to impose an income tax and we came to it later very gradually. Somebody suggests that it would have stopped the war if we had raised the whole of the debt at that time from an income tax. Perhaps, but we did not do so and we have been very cautious in extending it. I think here I shall have to commend the late government that they did not yield when considerable pressure was brought to bear upon them to wipe out that tax 'altogether, but rather held out for it. My contention is that it ought now to be greatly extended and that the major part of the revenues of this country should be raised through income taxation rather than, as it is to-day, through indirect taxation which -bears so heavily upon the people. In this I agree with the hon. member for AVeyburn (Mr. Young), and if he and other members on this side of the house would join with me, we would get a great deal further in raising a larger proportion of our revenue through the income tax which ought to be more steeply graded than it is at present. If that were done the $750,000 now proposed to be spent on technical education would be a mere bagatelle.
Another source of revenue that we might use is an inheritance tax. This is being practised to a considerable extent in Great Britain and I do not see why we should not adopt it in this country.

I would double,

Years ago it was stated in the manifesto of the Labour party-in Great Britain: We have gone on the principle that our death duties should take a very small percentage off and the greater part should be passed on to the heirs. We should go rather on the other principle that naked a man came into the world and naked he should go out. We should proceed on the principle of allowing an individual simply a sufficient amount of money to educate his family and provide for his dependents, the rest to be retained by the state for state purposes. If we were doing that in this country, we would not need to worry about spending $750,000 on technical education.
What does technical education mean? If we are to progress in Canada and take our place with the other great nations of the world, we must spend a great deal more than three-quarters of a million dollars a year on technical education. We ought to pour our millions into that work, if we would place ourselves beside other nations which have developed to such a great degree.
Mr. ST-PERE:	The province of Quebec
is already spending money on technical education.

maintopic: VOCATIONAL EDUCATION

speechtext:
Yes, and the other provinces too. But instead of talking about economizing in these matters, we should rather vie with one another as to how much we can spend when every cent that we spend is going into the lives of our children and into the building up of a finer and better nation.
I know there are theoretical objections which may be and which have been raised this afternoon, but such matters can be straightened out when a conference has been called. That should have been called ten years ago, but it has been put off and put off. I hope the present government will call it in the near future. In the meantime I would say that the quickest way to get a conference is to break in on the British North America Act in this manner, and then when the conference comes, we shall be more inclined to make even greater modifications of that act. The quickest way to get the proper adjustment of taxation is to spend and spend until the people generally wake up to the fact that they have to adopt means of taxation other than those which have so far been adopted in this country.

speechtext: I have frequently listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who has just spoken, and always with a great deal of respect. I should like to say to him to-day that while I have never questioned his sincerity, I believe he would have a great deal more influence in the house if he did not do quite so much scolding in both the manner of his presentation and the tone of his voice. The house will perhaps be surprised that I should make remarks of this kind because I very seldom do so. The hon. member has seen fit to read a lecture to both the Liberals and the farmers in this house. He has referred to the Liberal party in England-and I have no special brief for that party-as being a dying institution. Perhaps that is so, but he might indulge in a little self-examination as to why, as he says, the Liberal party in England is dying and the Labour party is apparently taking its place-

But I do. I have nothing
to say against the Labour party because I am just as strong an advocate of the rights of labour as he is, although perhaps he will not admit it. I may ask: whereas the Liberal party in England is apparently going down and the Labour party is going up, why in the world does the same thing not happen in Canada? Perhaps after all, the Labour party in England is well led and I would put the stress upon the word "England". I say that in all kindness to my hon. friend and I hope he will so consider it.
Just a word in regard to the merits of the question itself. I know it is more or less dangerous for any hon. member to place himself in a position which might be interpreted as opposed to technical education. I believe every hon. member, myself included, is in favour of technical education, and after all, the only question is as to who should carry out the work. My attitude is simply this-and I think it is eminently reasonable: education is a matter for the provinces. Constitutionally the provinces are charged with the work of education. That being the case, why should we depart from that principle? I am entirely'in favour of technical education, but unless there is some special reason why the federal parliament should intrude upon the rights and responsibilities of the provincial parliaments, I see no ground why in this particular instance we should violate that principle.

Vocational Education
The leader of the opposition has advanced an argument which to me has always seemed strong, so far as contributions to the provincial treasuries are concerned. He has stated that the debt of Canada is enormous, which is true, as a result chiefly of the war, and that our responsibilities by way of expenditures and taxation are exceptionally great. It cannot be successfully contradicted, that the financial responsibilities of the Dominion parliament are infinitely greater than those of any of the provinces. The province of Ontario and the province of Qudbec, comparatively speaking, are rich provinces and can well afford to carry out the obligations that are imposed upon them by the constitution. I am in favour of technical education, but I believe that we ought to keep things in their proper compartments, and if the duty of furnishing technical education or education of any other kind is imposed upon the provinces by the constitution, then why in the world should we depart from that? Each should discharge its own responsibility. The father is supposed to take care of his child. It it comes to want, if it needs assistance, its father, and not the father of somebody else, is supposed to take care of it. That is a homely illustration, but I think it holds good. It is merely a question of who should discharge the responsibility, and my argument is that the responsibility is placed upon the provinces, and I can see no good reason-certainly none has so far been advanced-why we should assume a responsibility that is strictly placed upon others, and who can afford to discharge it.

May I offer just a word,

This I will say in regard to his address, that the attitude which he has taken to-day in regard to the proposal to make federal grants in aid of technical education in the various provinces has been pretty consistent with his whole course since this question was first brought to the attention of the federal parliament, for I well remember that when I moved for
the first time in this parliament a quarter of a century ago for the appointment of a commission to inquire into technical education, my right hon. friend the present leader of the opposition was the one who moved a motion which killed mine, and I was the only one then on the Liberal side who voted in favour of such a commission. However, a year or so afterwards, he decided that the popular demand in favour of something being done by the federal government was so great that it was time to act. and my right hon. friend, who was then Minister of Labour in the Liberal administration of that day, did issue a commission for the purpose of inquiring into technical education, and that commission made a very valuable report to parliament.
During the course of his remarks to-day the right hon. leader of the opposition alluded to the late Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, one of the most eminent finance ministers that Canada has ever produced, a man who for fifteen years was finance minister in the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and was afterwards for five years finance minister in the government of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT

speechtext: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 41, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext: I understand that this bill contains only one provision, the purpose of which is to change the personnel of the board and to appoint a commissioner. Probably the minister would make a short explanation of the bill.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext:
The bill has for its purpose the abolition of the present board which now consists of a chairman and two members. The intention is to substitute for the board

Soldier Settlement Act
a single individual who, it is suggested, should be called the director of soldier settlement. The reason for the amendment to the Soldier Settlement Act of 1919 contemplated by this bill is that at the present time the board is not acquiring any further land. The work of the board in a great measure has decreased but there has not been any corresponding decrease in the administrative staff. At the present time the head office is at Ottawa, and by reason of having three commissioners on the board nine separate branches are necessary at the head office. Each branch performs work of a similar character, and a great deal of overlapping takes place. With a single director there will be an immediate saving of administrative expense in connection with the board alone of about $26,000. Under the leadership of a single director there will be required only three branches at the head office, namely, the accounts branch, the agricultural branch and the estates and securities branch. The other districts throughout Canada will be made to conform to the organization at the head office, and the total yearly administrative expense will be reduced. I believe the result will be greater efficiency in the administration of the affairs of the board, and a reduction in cost of over a quarter of a million dollars. I am convinced that this reorganization should take place, and that greater efficiency would be the result.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Is it the
intention of the government to confer more power, so far as accounting is concerned, upon district inspectors, or as heretofore, will the accounting all be done in the offices in Ottawa? I believe the minister mentioned some powers which would be transferred.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT

speechtext: I notice the commissioner of the board means the director of soldier settlement under this section, while under section 1, "board" means the director of soldier settlement. Is there not some inconsistency between the two sections?

speechtext: The reason the commissioner of the board is interpreted to mean the director of soldier settlement is because there are a number of places in the act of 1919, which is being amended, where certain powers of the board are delegated to a commissioner of the board, as for instance in sections 55 and 56. In order to vest in the director of soldier settlement all the authority the board had, acting as a board, and all the authority of the board acting through one of its members, it was necessary to insert that clause in the interpretation of this amending bill, making the commissioner and the board mean the director.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext:
But under section 1
"board" means the director of soldier settlement. Is there not an inconsistency between the two? In one case "director" means the whole board, and in the next section it means the commissioner, which I assume to be only part of the board.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Let me try to make that clear. Section 3 of the Soldier Settlement Act of 1919 provided:
The soldier settlement board, as constituted pursuant to the former act. . . .
That was the act of 1917.
.... shall continue to consist of three commissioners, each to hold office during good behaviour, but to be removable by the governor in council at any time for cause and to become ineligible upon attaining seventy years of age.
In order to substitute the director of soldier settlement for the board as contemplated by the law, section 1 is inserted. Then I turn to section 56 of the act being amended, which is a good illustration of why the further interpretation was given. Section 56 reads:
Any commissioner of the board, or any officer or employee of the board authorized, specifically or generally, in writing, by a commissioner of the board ....
The amendment contemplates that the director shall not only have all the powers and
Soldier Settlement Act

privileges of the board acting as such, but also those of any commissioner of the board to whom the board might delegate power. The board has the right to delegate its powers under the act, in certain circumstances, to one Df themselves, and the amendment has in contemplation that all those powers and privileges now shall be vested in the one director of soldier settlement.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext: Will the full power at present vested in the board be turned over to this director? The board really functions as two separate bodies, though with the same personnel. The one Body deals with soldier settlement matters, while the other deals with general land settlement matters. Under that branch comes the three thousand family scheme, for example and various other branches of settlement. I notice in the act this official is referred to as the director of soldier settlement only. I wonder if the dual functions of the board will be vested in this new director, and if he will carry on the work of general land settlement as well as the soldier settlement work.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext:
The director of soldier
settlement, by this bill, will be vested with the same powers heretofore possessed by the board or any commissioner of the board.

maintopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT
speechtext:
My question has
reference to section 1, which has been declared carried. refer to the act of 1919 he will see that the word "board" is there interpreted to mean the Soldier Settlement Board of Canada. Subsection 1 of the amending act merely interprets the board to mean the director of soldier settlement, following exactly the same phraseology.

On section 3-Appointment of director.

speechtext:

no changes here?

speechtext:

clause with respect to the salary of the director of soldier settlement. All his functions

my hon: friend that there should be adequate remuneration.
