maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE, FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE for the Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE, FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity once more to impress upon the government the urgent necessity of holding a conference with the provinces in connection with the subject of unemployment. I have brought this subject up several times already, and I would not bring it up again if it were not that in addition to the facts that I presented before there has since been a growing weight of circumstances, and also a very definite growth of public sentiment.
On the 31st of March I said:
I believe that next winter the unemployment situation will be worse than it was last year.
Events are rapidly corroborating that statement. I also referred to the fact that a delegation had gone down from Nanaimo to Victoria asking the provincial government what they were going to do to relieve the situation in the coal mining area, which was then in a very bad condition. It has got worse since. I also mentioned that Premier Tolmie was going to come down to Ottawa to ask that $100,000 be granted to the city of Vancouver, without the city being asked to contribute on
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

a fifty-fifty basis, because they were out of money and in a desperate condition. Later, on May 7, I called the attention of the house to the unemployment situation as regards the logging industry, and also to the fact that two towns in British Columbia, which I named, had advertised that men were not to come to those places because there were already 600 men looking for work and unable to obtain it. I ended by impressing upon the government the need for an immediate conference with the provinces on the question of unemployment. Apropos of this, the following headline appears in the evening papers to-day:
Winnipeg Jobless Wreck Labour-Saving Machine
That shows what me.n will do when they are desperate. We will go across the continent, beginning with Winnipeg. The following appeared recently:
Hon. W. R. Clubb. Minister of Public Works, is on his way to Ottawa to urge the Dominion government to continue direct unemployed relief during the summer months.
It will be noticed that that refers to the summer months. Before we were discussing winter relief, but we have to face an immediate situation. The report continues:
He will also ask for a readjustment of the basis upon which the relief has been granted.
We come next to Vancouver, where the following was published:
Expenditures of the city relief department in the first four months of this year amounted to $290,403, which is $27,103 more than the sum estimated for the period.
The report continues:
Estimates and expenditures are as follows:
For April:
April, estimate, $43,700; expenditure, $56,545.
That is a month when ordinarily there would be little or no relief required. The report continues:
The relief officer drew the committee's attention to the "continued serious condition of unemployment in the city." Instead of the usual seasonal improvement in April he said there appears to have been a decrease in the number of men employed in Vancouver. Dominion reports, he said, show a decrease of almost 1,700 workers in that period.
These conditions, said the officer, are reflected in the department's records; and since April 1 married unemployed cases have increased to 1,346, an advance of 269. This total, he said, is greater than any in the past winter.
Note that. The report continues:
The city has already drawn this situation to the attention of the federal and provincial governments. remarking that the city cannot adequately cope with it. Acknowledgment of the letter was received, but no further progress has been made.
[Mr. Neill.)
Hence the necessity for bringing this matter before the house. The report continues:
"The present situation shows that the council's forecast was only too correct," states Colonel Cooper. "The city's inability to cope with the situation is even more pronounced than on March 28. I would, therefore, recommend that the strongest possible representations be made, in order to convince the governments of the need for prompt and effective [DOT] action."
Then we have the mayor of Vancouver, a man of some repute, reported in Winnipeg as follows:
Admitting a national responsibility, Premier Bennett should call the governments of the four western provinces and the mayors of the larger cities to an unemployment conference, Mayor L. D. Taylor of Vancouver stated in an interview here last night. If Premier Bennett refuses to call such a conference, Mayor Taylor declared that he and Mayor R. H. Webb, of Winnipeg would themselves take the responsibility of calling this meeting early in July at either Edmonton or Calgary, whichever city was most convenient for those taking part.
The report continues:
The unemployment situation in western Canada, he told Mr. Bennett, was likely to remain acute "for at least another year," and everybody should recognize it as a national emergency, he declared, and act accordingly.
The city of Vancouver, he told Mr. Bennett, was willing to care for its own. But last winter it had had 10,000 unemployed single men who are non-residents to feed and house. In fifteen months the city had paid $1,000,000 for emergency relief. It could not shoulder this burden for another year.
We should have an adequate program of public works to be carried on throughout the west. This is the belief of Mayor Taylor of Vancouver and of Mayor Webb of Winnipeg, the latter being a well-known friend of the government of the day. The next report comes from Saanich, a semi-rural and semiurban municipality on Vancouver island, and reads as follows:
The problem of unemployment will be much more serious next winter than it was last year.
Then we come to Nanaimo. I received the following telegram from the president of the board of trade of Nanaimo:
Local conditions very serious. Seven hundred eighty men out employment in this district. City Nanaimo near . end of its resources. Council, board trade and merchants met Hon. Bruhn, Minister of Public Works last night. Minister fully understands seriousness situation due to non-operation coal mines and realizes that immediate action necessary but cannot take any steps alleviate situation until federal government decide what proportion inevitable burden they are going assume.
I brought that matter up in the house yesterday and received the usual stereotyped reply that if something else happened some-

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
thing else would happen; that it was a "purely provincial matter", and "that if it is found that the municipal and provincial authorities cannot relieve the situation, there is no doubt that proper steps will be taken, and taken without delay, by this government, to assist." The government has been told time and again that this situation exists. The word of a minister of the crown in the province of British Columbia should not be treated lightly when he says the condition requires alleviation. A report in this connection reads as follows:
The Hon. R. W. Bruhn, Minister of Public Works in the provincial government, paid a visit to the city yesterday, and last night in the city hall, met a large delegation consisting of members of the city council, members of the Retail Merchants' Association, and members of the board of trade.
The chairman stated that there was no immediate hope or prospect of any improvement in the situation, and asked the assistance of the government. The city, he said, had done what it could, and was still prepared to do what it could, but the government would have to find relief for these men out of work. The report continues:
Mr. Bruhn explained that he was quite familiar with the facts of the situation, and realized that something would have to be done and at once. The provincial government was prepared to do its part, but was seeking the cooperation of the federal government. He had sent telegrams to Ottawa but had as yet received no definite reply upon which action could be taken. He could promise nothing until the return of Premier Tolmie, and he could not see that the province could undertake any further relief work until the federal government promised to do its share.
I suggest that some kind of political tracer be sent out to locate this Hon. Mr. Tolmie, because he seems to be lost. Where is our wandering boy to-night? He is not here and he does not appear to be there; he does not appear to be anywhere when he is urgently needed. If he is a requisite necessity in the program, by all means let us get hold of him at any cost. Another local man of good standing reported that the situation is appalling because of the coal mines having been shut down. The same situation obtains at Cumberland-which is in my district and in which I am naturally most interested-where one of the mines have been shut down. They have appealed to the government but have been informed that nothing can be done until some remote and distant period. We now come to Victoria where the Hon. W. A. McKenzie, who is I understand the chairman of the government committee dealing with unemployment, is reported on March 12 as having said:
A national conference on unemployment to be held at the earliest possible date, and to line
up plans for handling unemployment relief next winter, was urged in a government statement by Hon. W. A. McKenzie, Minister of Labour.
"Now is the time to shape these preparations and the sooner a conference, national in scope, is called, the better," Mr. McKenzie said.
"What we should do at this time of the year, when unemployment is least serious, is to consider as a nation what we should and what we can do to relieve unemployment in the slack winter months. There is no use putting our heads in the sand like ostriches, as if no unemployment problem would face us again. We look for improving conditions and believe the improvement has set in, but it will be the worst kind of folly to make no plans this summer for meeting an unemployment situation next w'inter. Let us face this issue and line up definite programs which can be put into prompt and efficient operation if and when the necessity arises."
That is from Victoria, the head of the government, and at least one of the prominent men in it. That is the situation. We find these four cities in British Columbia, and also the city of Winnipeg, which is a very large one, asking not only for some action for next winter but for immediate relief and for the calling of a conference at once. They do not want it next winter or next fall; they want it now, and they say so at length. More than that, they say that some definite allotment of the money will have to be arranged. The cities are not now able to put up 50 per cent of the cost, and it is no use disguising that fact. In British Columbia we are limited by law to a certain amount that we can borrow in proportion to our assessment rolls. Many of the cities have reached that point and they cannot legally borrow more. Where are they to find the money? That situation has to be faced between the provinces and the Dominion, and the sooner it is faced, the better.
There is another thing that will have to be attended to. For example, in the little town in which I live the provincial government, in my opinion, imposed upon us a condition not required by the federal regulations. The undertaking was that we should pay 50 per cent of the cost of the relief work, the province 25 per cent and the Dominion 25 per cent. What did the province do? I cannot find it in any regulation made by this government, and the regulations were printed and distributed. We were compelled to put up all the cost of the material. If we built a sidewalk, we had to put up the whole of the cost of the ldmber and we were given only 50 per cent of the labour cost. I cannot find any provision of this kind in the act. I cannot say that this was graft, because it was not graft in the sense of somebody making money by it, but it was a gross injustice to the smaller towns, and I hope when we are discussing the sub-
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

jeot of the distribution of more money, we shall be protected. I warned the government at the time that they should keep the control in their own hands, and then they would be responsible. Very little complaint can be made against this government in connection with the way the money was handled, because they gave it to the provinces, and then when we come with our complaints, they say, as I predicted they would: It is the provinces that are handling the money; we cannot control them. In some cases the Dominion officials acted promptly when a complaint was made to them for the purpose of investigation, but it was the provinces who used the money unfairly and politically.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE, FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was that done by the municipalities? _
Mr, NEILL:	No, the municipalities ran
:hing3 fairly. This was outside of the municipalities in what is known as unorganized territory and it was done by the province. In the municipalities it was run all right, because they comprised men on both sides of politics. The municipalities did it fairly and squarely; I have not a thing to say against their conduct.
My suggestion is that the conference should be held now, for two reasons: first, to deal with the immediate distress, the distress that is now existing in some parts of the country; and,' second, to formulate some scheme to handle the relief that will undoubtedly be needed next winter, and vote the' necessary funds. It may be said that it is useless to have this conference now as regards next winter; that we can have it after the house has prorogued. If we wait until parliament

prorogues, where are we going to get the money next winter?-because it will be not $20,000,000 but $30,000,000 that will be required. Assuming, however, that $20,000,000 will be required, and parliament prorogues without voting it, where are we to get the money? The obvious answer of course will be by governor general's warrant. But the government could not take that position, because that is the very opposite of the position they took last year. It was thrown up to me time and again in the election that I was not in favour of holding an immediate sitting of the house to vote money for relief. I said that this could be done by governor general's warrant, and this was made the subject of an attack upon me. Surely we cannot conclude that the government will now turn around and do the very thing they rejected last year. If they do so they would be admitting that the session held last September was needless and a wasteful expense. Where is the money to be found if it is not voted before parliament prorogues?
Those are the two reasons on which I base my demand, without any political aspect to the matter at all. A further" reason why we should have the conference now while the house is sitting is that it would have the advantage of the presence in Ottawa of able men-whether they 'belong to one party or the other, it matters not-from the various provinces, who could give the local information needed. For these reasons I wish to impress upon the government the necessity of an immediate conference, in order to give immediate assistance, in order to arrange for a winter program, and in order to have the money voted while we are here to vote >t.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE, FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) when he has to bring this matter up on the motion to go into supply, has evidently despaired of getting any satisfactory answer from the government with respect to their attitude on unemployment. During this session some attempts have been made, but without much success, to ascertain the attitude of the government. I can recall at the moment the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asking several times what the government proposed to do with respect to unemployment, but he received no reply. In fact, instead of an answer there was a show of complete indifference with respect to the question. When on one occasion I tried to discuss the subject in the house there was a report in the press to the effect that 6,000 unemployed had paraded in Winnipeg. At

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
that time the house ruled against me; it decided that this was not a question of national importance.
To what the hon. member for Comox-Al-berni has said I can add by saying that I have a knowledge of what has transpired in my own district. In the towns of Kenora and Fort Frances there are hundreds of un. employed, although those towns are not very large centres. Moreover, we have the spectacle of the provincial government appropriating only S5.000.000 for highway construction this year, whereas last year, just prior to the . election, they appropriated 810,000,000. We have endeavoured to elicit from the federal government some indication of what they are going to do in connection with highway construction as was promised by them during the election, but we have not succeeded in getting it. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, therefore, is quite justified in bringing the matter up on the motion to go into supply, not, as I understand it, as a vote of feck of confidence in the government, but to try to ascertain just what the government proposes to do with respect to this question.

speechtext: I did not move an amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE, FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unemployment-Mr. Maclnnis
This government, let me remind the house, was elected on a definite pledge to end unemployment. Up to the present time, since the government has come into office, unemployment has increased rather than decreased. Alter the government gave that pledge to the electors to end unemployment, and assumed the responsibility of office, after their declaration that unemployment relief was not a provincial or municipal obligation, but a national obligation, why are they now simply waiting, sitting in their seats, and not telling the house and the country what attitude they are going to take with respect to unemployment? I had always thought that unemployment relief was a question for the municipalities and the provinces. In that regard I followed the lead of the ex-premier of Ontario, Mr. Howard Ferguson, who invariably declined to look upon it as other than a municipal obligation. We have sufficient evidence of that. Then in 1921 we had the Conservative government passing an order in council which began by stating that the unemployment question was a provincial and a municipal responsibility. When the Conservative party appealed to the electors in 1930 they declared that this was not a provincial or a municipal responsibility at all, but a federal responsibility. But the very first act of the new government, at the special session last September, was to bring in a bill which on the face of it declared that the question was a municipal and a provincial one.
Unemployment is undoubtedly on the increase. We have the government's own statistics to prove that. There is suffering all over the country. The hon. member for Comox-Aiberni has told us quite plainly of the suffering entailed in some parts of the country. I have spoken of the suffering in northern Ontario, where delegations have gone down from some of the towns to Toronto to interview the provincial government. I might mention the town of Sturgeon Falls, the town of Espanola. In my own town of Kenora and in Fort Frances, the pulp mills are working about only one month out of the whole twelve. And mind you, that is because of the attitude of the provincial government. The provincial government has agreements with these industrial concerns which obligates them to work ten months in each and every year, yet for some reason or other they have released these concerns from their obligation as contained in those agreements, so I think the provincial government must assume some responsibility to the citizens of that part of the country.

But apart from all that, the federal Conservative party is undoubtedly on record as declaring to the electors of this country that if they were elected in 1930 they would take upon themselves the responsibility of curing unemployment as a national problem. Yet only the other day the minister stated on the. floor of this house, in answer to a question from the hon. member for Comox-Aiberni, that undoubtedly, as no doubt the house understood, this was a provincial and a municipal responsibility.
I was struck with the argument of my right hon. leader this afternoon when he pointed out that wherever there is a division of authority, with one party passing the buck to someone else, we never get anywhere. Today we find provinces that will not inaugurate old age pensons, believing that it is a federal responsibility. Because the federal government first of all contributed 50 per cent of the old age pensions, some of the provinces now want the federal government to contribute 100 per cent. But the worst feature of all is this, that we find provincial governments, like the government of Ontario, for instance, refusing to go on with provincial undertakings unless the federal government contributes a proportion of the cost. That is a position which they never took before.
The question which has been brought up by my hon. friend from Comox-Aiberni is deserving of an answer from the government. So far as I am concerned I consider that the federal government should do what they promised to do-take the responsibility of finding employment for the workpeople of Canada, of dealing with the unemployed, and of bringing in a system of unemployment insurance in order to take care of our Workpeople when unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add
a few words to what has been said by the hon. member for Comox-Aiberni (Mr. Neill) concerning the unemployment situation in British Columbia and particularly in regard to the city of Vancouver. speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, May 5,' consideration, of the motion of Mr. Woods-worth for the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the criminal code.
Mr. ANGUS MaeINNIS (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) I should like to say a few words in support of this bill.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in bringing forward this amendment, made certain references to what had taken place in certain cities of this dominion in reference to free assembly and free speech, with particular reference to the city of Toronto. It is very difficult to deal with this amendment without knowing really what occurred in that city.
It has been suggested by some who are opposing the amendment that there is a section of the criminal code having to do with unlawful assembly which is quite sufficient as it now stands. I am almost inclined to believe that is quite correct, but the difficulty we find here is that the police commissioners in many cities suspend, as it were, the criminal code as far as unlawful assembly is concerned and make rules and regulations of their own to cover the circumstances -of the case. The code, as I see it, lays down that the gathering itself and what is said at the gathering must be the criterion for a conclusion as to whether or not the assembly is unlawful. However, unless a meeting is allowed to take place I cannot see how it possibly can be said to be an unlawful assembly. There is a provision in the code itself for preventing gatherings under certain conditions-section 99-and the procedure is by proclamation of the governor in council. If it is intended, therefore, that any authority should set aside any section of the criminal code, that action should be done in the same manner, by proclamation of the governor in council.
As to what really was intended in the city of Toronto I should like again to draw attention to a quotation made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in this connection. I refer to a letter from Colonel Biggar, formerly chief electoral officer. Before a person can qualify as a candidate during a federal election there are very strict regulations with which he must comply. Having done so he has fulfilled the law and is entitled to stand
1984	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
as a candidate for election to the Dominion parliament, and it is taken for granted, I believe, that he is entitled to express his opinion on the public platform at least in the constituency in which he is standing for election. In Toronto this right was interfered with. The quotation I wish to give from Colonel Biggar's letter is as follows:
The real question raised by these and Mr. Cohen's present letter is the question whether in Toronto the police are enforcing the law or are persecuting persons who hold opinions of which they disapprove, by the confiscation of printed matter found in their possession, by physical violence, by the misuse of licensing [DOT] powers, and by threat of the institution of criminal proceedings for which there is no foundation.
I am not quite sure whether the amendment will help clarify the section in reference to unlawful assembly in order to cover a case of this kind, but I rather think this Dominion was fortunate in having a man like Colonel Biggar as chief electoral officer. He drew the attention of the police of the city of Toronto to what they could and could not do in connection with preventing the gathering of people who did not hold the same views as they held.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), in opposing this bill said as follows, at page 1277 of Hansard:
I submit to you, sir, and to the hon. members of this house, that the law as it now stands is perfectly clear and needs no clarifying, and further. that the privileges of any honest citizen in this country are to-day amply safeguarded under the existing provisions of the criminal code.
It seems that according to the police in Toronto, an honest citizen is anyone who holds the same opinions held by the police commissioners, and consequently it follows that all the others are dishonest. I understand that the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) was asked to address the Canadian Club in Toronto. At the same time he was asked to address another association, the Fellowship of Reconciliation. He was allowed to address the Canadian Club, but the other association could not get a hall in which to hold its meeting. I take it that not only were the privileges of this association interfered with, but that the privileges of the hon. member for Bow River were also interfered with.

subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: Anyone who has knowledge to the contrary may say so, but in the meantime I think my statement stands.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
What was the nature of the
interference?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
They could not get a
hall in which to meet. That is the point I wish to make; the privileges of citizens are being interfered with. Later on, the hon. member for Northumberland, N. B. (Mr. MeDade), speaking against the amendment, questioned the right of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for North Winnipeg to speak for what he called that large section of the community known 'as the labour element. I do not think the member for Winnipeg North Centre put forward the amendment in the interest of any class, but rather in the interest of what we always used to term the British institutions of free assembly and free speech. The hon. member for Northumberland, N.B., referred to two other citizens from his province and said:
I would far rather take the advice and counsel of such outstanding labour men in the province of New Brunswick as Mr. John S. Martin, former Labour member of the legislative assembly at Fredericton, or of Mr. Stanley S. Fleiger, of the town of Chatham, than that of my hon. friends opposite. The men I have mentioned, I submit, represent true Canadian labour; their judgment is sound and their capacity is unquestioned.
I think those of us who know both the member for Winnipeg North Centre and the member for North Winnipeg will agree that their views are sound, and that at least, with the exception of one other, they are the only representatives that labour definitely has in this house.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
However, I am going to read parts of a letter received from Mr. John S. Martin, one of the persons mentioned by the hon. member for Northumberland, to show that he and other Labour men in New Brunswick agree with the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
The letter is dated May 14, 1931, is addressed to Mr. J. S. Woodsworth and, in part, is as follows:
The reason for this letter arose from the debate in the house on Tuesday, May 6, re your amendment to the Criminal Code. My name as well as the name of a particular friend of mine, Stanley Fleiger, was mentioned by the member for our county, Northumberland. His remarks might lead you to believe that he was authorized to use our names and that he was further authorized to speak for Labour. Such is not the case.
1 am a vice-president of the New Brunswick Federation of Labour for the northern section of the province and you have my support in the bill you presented as well as in any other efforts you put forward in behalf of the workers notwithstanding what any party politician may have said in the past or may say in the future.
The fact that my name was brought into the debate only came to my' attention to-day. I immediately 'phoned the president of the New' Brunsw'ick Federation of Labour, Mr. Eugene Steeves of Moncton, and w-as informed by him that your amendment to the Criminal Code has his hearty support. So you are now' aware that you had a right to speak for Labour in the province of New' Brunsw'ick as well as other sections of Canada. . . .
Now, sir, what I have said re your right to speak for Labour in this section is endorsed by Stanley Fleiger, the other name mentioned by Mr. McDade.
You are at liberty to use, if you so desire, anything that I have written in this letter in part or whole, and if at any time you should want information on any matter in this section I will be pleased to assist in any way I can.
I am sure that if at any time you pay a visit to this province I will be very glad to make arrangements so that you can meet the people whom you represent.
John S. Martin.
Now, I do not think that letter should leave any doubt in the minds of anyone as to whom the member for Winnipeg North Centre is representing not only in his own constituency but in various other parts of the Dominion. A3 I said before, the amendment will help to clarify the section in regard to unlawful assembly. But what, I think, is needed more than anything else is someone in authority who will inform the police commissioners in our various cities that they cannot at their will and pleasure thrust aside the laws of this land and make regulations to suit their own purposes.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, it seems to me a strange thing that if you happen to be of some particular church persuasion or of some well-known political affiliation freedom of speech is accorded you almost without any restriction, but if you happen to be the member of a labour party or one of the independent groups that freedom of speech is sometimes criticized and it is
suggested that it would be better if you were put under a ban. Fortunately most of us do not live in a city so convinced of its own righteousness as the city of Toronto. In most parts of this country we are, comparatively speaking, free to express our viewpoint upon conditions and upon affairs that are before the public for consideration. But it seems that in the city of Toronto you endanger almost your liberty-yes, you do endanger your liberty if you express any radical views on almost any matter whatever. At the same time you will find men like Mr. Beatty going up there and giving expression to a thought on the cancellation of war debts and getting away with it; but if we even here in the House of Commons suggested the cancellation of war debts-as we did in 1923-we are assailed both by hon. members and by the press as being unpatriotic, as being quite disloyal citizens and unworthy of the positions that we hold. Words to exactly that effect were used about us when we did make that recommendation. I looked with interest to the Mail and Empire, the Orange Sentinel, the Globe and one or two other strange publications from that city in order to find some criticism of Mr. Beatty's radical utterance, but there was only praise for a statesmanlike pronouncement of a policy that should have been expressed long ago!
Some years ago I clipped from the Manitoba Free Press a paragraph which at that time interested me enormously. I found that in Winnipeg at any rate one could express himself with the utmost freedom, one could urge sedition, one could say, for example, that no great social or economic change had ever been accomplished in any nation of the world without revolution, without overthrowing constituted authority,-and all this, if you please, at a meeting of some society for the celebration of St. George's day. Let me give the house an idea of what some people can get away with, but what, economic students or those who are considering the actual conditions that face the common people and trying to propose remedies for them must not speak-at least in Toronto, with its police force under the commissionership of a gentleman who has no more understanding of economics or the effect of them on the people than perhaps have some hon. gentlemen in this house.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me? Has anybody ever stopped my hon. friend from addressing the Canadian club in Toronto?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
No. You see, the, Canadian club there is a respectable body,
19S6

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
and I must say it is also a very hospitable body and a very attentive body-and apparently a very intelligent body even for Toronto.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: Did the hon. member make any converts there?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I doubt
it very much. However, there is always hope, because it is not so many years since the hon. member himself would hardly have said the same things that he is quite willing to say to-day-at least after dinner. Mr. R. B. Graham, K.C., a fairly well known gentleman-[DOT]

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: A magistrate.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Yes, I
am informed he is a magistrate now. He was proposing the toast to "England" before the Royal St. George society. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) will appreciate that it is all right before audiences of this kind to say quite violent things, but one must not say them at labour meetings; that is altogether improper. Let me read this clipping:
The occasion was the annual St. George's night dinner of the society over which the president, Jackson Dodds, O.B.E., presided as chairman.
I understand that Mr. Jackson Dodds is also a very respectable man. He is, I think, the president or vice president of the bankers' association, or something like that.
Music was furnished during and after the dinner-
So you see they stayed while the speeches were being made.
-by the regimental band of Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry-
And by one or two other gentlemen who contributed solos. The address delivered by this gentleman in the presence of these august and representative Canadian citizens was in the following terms:
No nation ever became truly great save by successful sedition and revolution. The lamp and the torch and the tumult have overcome tyranny. The signature of King John was placed to the Magna Charta, wrenched from him by the nobles; revolution led King Charles to the block; the corn law riots-these were crimes against the law and seditions, but no one hangs his head in shame because of them. "Liberty, equality, fraternity," were no mere catchwords as in the French revolution, but the expression of the earnest striving for the substance that lies behind the words.
I submit that if any member of the Labour party in this house used words of that kind in Toronto he would be put in gaol. It was riots which brought about these improve-
'Mr. E. J. Garland.]
ments of economic conditions and, as I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said already, it may require riots to bring some indication of appreciation of conditions to hon. members of this house, particularly on the government side. We have an illustration appearing in the newspapers. Fifteen hundred men applied for a job in Winnipeg which had been advertised as requiring one hundred men. Fourteen hundred men were disappointed, and what did they do? There was a riot and they broke up the machines. The only thing which relieves such pressure is the possibility on the part of the people concerned of discussing their problems. Continue the policy of the suppression of free speech and as surely as I am standing here you will drive underground and make stronger the forces antagonistic to society, as has been evidenced here. One of the finest outlets for this pressure is to have some form of safety valve such as is found in freedom of discussion.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Did these men have a trial?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
If my hon. friend the Deputy Speaker (Mr. LaVergne), who is so bitter in matters relating to labour problems, free speech, and the socialization of conditions as we have them to-day, would be more tolerant and less like Toronto, his utterances in this country would be restored to their old virility.
Mr. LaVERGNE: The hon. member must be mistaken, because I am in favour of the bill. I was just wanting to know whether these men had had a trial in Toronto.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Whether
they were tried in Toronto?
Mr. LaVERGNE: Yes.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
No.
Mr. LaVERGNE: How could they have been arrested and not have had a trial?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
These men were not arrested at all. I am giving an illustration of how you can get away with it if you are a "respectable" person appearing before a "respectable" audience, but if you happen to be a labour man addressing a labour audience, particularly in Toronto, you would be put behind the bars for using the very words employed in this instance. I am satisfied that if the inward thoughts, and sometimes the privately uttered thoughts, of many of the hon members of this house on

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
both sides were made public, in Toronto, the hon. members concerned would be in danger of being put in gaol.
The purpose of the hon. member in introducing this amendment is to make it clear to police commissions and to the cities that Canada intends to pursue the old British ideal of free speech and liberty to express one's thoughts so long as they do not urge armed revolution or direct action at the moment. Permission is to be given to people to endeavour to convert others to their philosophy, whether it be the Russian philosophy, to which my hon. friend takes objection, or a philosophy atheistic in character so long as it is not calculated to be a breach of the peace. Free speech should be permitted in this country.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Is there not a statute in Ontario-there is one in Quebec-under which any meeting could be made legal?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I am not a lawyer and I have not had time to look into all the statutes. I only know the facts. A respectable body of citizens in the city of Toronto-the city has gone to extremes in this respect-composed of such well known and splendid characters as Doctor Salem Bland, Rabbi Eisendrath and others, was prevented from securing a suitable hall in which to hold a meeting. This organization, known as the Fellowship of Reconciliation, was compelled to cancel its meeting.
Mr. LaVERGNE: How .could they be prevented?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
They were prevented.
Mr. LaVERGNE: No one is obliged to rent a hall.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
From his last statement it would seem the hon. gentleman has not been listening to this debate with the same care evidenced by others. I think the hon. gentleman who preceded me, the introducer of the amendment (Mr. Woodsworth), pointed out that by devious methods the police commission of Toronto revoked the licences of the owners or renters of the halls in which it was intended to have meetings of this or other organizations.
Mr. LaVERGNE: There must be a redress in law somewhere,

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
It may be found that the police commission of Toronto broke the law in taking this action, but they took it.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, I intend to say only a sentence or two in support of the principle of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). It happens that I am one of the people who were refused permission to speak in a hall in the city of Toronto, although at almost the same time I addressed different clubs in that city. The difficulty occurred when the Fellowship of Reconciliation attempted to rent a hall in which to have a public meeting to be cddressed by me. I should like to think I was a dangerous person if that term means one who attempts to undo many of the things now existent in Canada. If that term means one who would assist to decentralize finance, for instance, then I should 'be glad to think I were a dangerous person. However, it might be considered as being conceited to think so, and I do not consider myself as such yet. I was refused the right to address a public meeting.
However, that is not the thought which persuaded me to make a few remarks in support of this bill. Whatever dangers there may be in free speech, and I suppose there are some, they are small indeed as compared to the dangers of the prohibition of free speech. I have always found, and I think other hon. members have had the same experience, that if people utter thoughts which are foolish, while a few people may believe them, in the long run they do not win out. It is sound common sense which wins in the end. I stand for free speech and the right of free assembly. If things are said at these assemblies which would constitute a breach of the peace, the law Can take its course and the offenders can be put where they may change or it is to be hoped they will change their minds.
I do not like to say it, but apparently there are hon. members in this house, and there certainly are people in the city of Toront? who think that communistic gatherings and propaganda can be stopped by prohibiting the right of assembly and free speech. That is utter nonsense. Communistic tendencies can be stopped by a return to prosperity, if anyone knows how to bring that about. People who are comfortable are not interested in communistic doctrines; it is the people who are uncomfortable who listen to sueh talk. The method adopted by the police commission of Toronto was an exceedingly foolish one. Ever since the person at the head of that commission took over his duties there has been one constant turmoil. He may have brought about one sort of peace, but he has

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
created a great deal of disorder in so doing. Apparently he was a man who was out to command, and he wanted everyone else to obey. I think the interference with free speech and assembly is being carried altogether too far. To my great surprise I found that even the liberal-minded city of Montreal had been following the lead given by Toronto, a thing I would never have suspected it of. Even on the prairies which one thinks of as the home of what radical thought we have in Canada, there has 'been a tendency to follow the lead given by the police commissioners of Toronto. So it is in protest against this that I say that I am most heartily in support of the bill of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth).

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: After all the things that have been said about the city of Toronto, I feel almost like coming to its defence. I was one of those who, like the previous speaker, had great difficulty in finding a place to hold a meeting. The reason I wish to say a word or two in defence of Toronto is because the day I arrived in that city I found that in one of the leading theatres a play written by none other than George Bernard Shaw, was being produced. When I saw that play, which is purely socialistic in its philosophy, produced by an English company, I was rather surprised that' the police commission of Toronto had overlooked the fact. Evidently there is still some idea of allowing something in the way of free speech in that city.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
What was the name of
the play?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: The Apple Cart. I was very agreeably surprised when I went into the theatre to see sitting not far from me a gentleman who no douibt has something to do with the suppression of free speech in Toronto. I refer to Sir William Mulock. Moreover, sitting in one of the boxes, enjoying the socialistic philosophy of George Bernard Shaw, was none other than the Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: Did they seem to be enjoying themselves?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
So far as I could make out
they seemed to be enjoying the play. So I want to say that in the city of Toronto both the humble and the rich can enjoy something in the way of free speech.
The question has been asked in the house, particularly by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) as to who prevented the obtaining of a hall in which to speak, or

at least the inference was that there was no interference by the police of Toronto in connection with the hiring of halls. I think in this instance the hon. member is not quite as fair as he usually is in regard to matters that come before the house.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Is the hon. member aware
of the fact that the Labour Temple, which is controlled by the Labour movement, refused to allow a meeting of this nature to be held there ?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: There is a difference between the owners of a hall of their own free will refusing to rent a hall for a meeting, and the chief of police or his representative going down to the owner of a hall and threatening him if a meeting is to be held there.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: That was not done.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
During the time the
hon. member was in the theatre, was he the guest of one of the Toronto members?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I certainly was. May I say
in answer to the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) that I will give him an incident with which I was personally connected. I was asked to speak at a certain hall in Toronto and before the hall was allowed to be used, the police went down to the hall and threatened the owners that if it was used for a meeting at which I was to speak, they would suffer as a consequence. In addition to that, when they defied the police and held the meeting in the hall, policemen actually came there to see what was going on, whether it was a peaceable meeting, I suppose, or otherwise. Strange as it may appear, when the police arrived at the hall where the meeting was taking place, the gentleman who happened to be speaking that night was none other than Controller Simpson of Toronto. I do not know who was more surprised, the police when they walked in and saw Controller Simpson, who was speaking, or Controller Simpson who was on the platform and saw the police walk in. I have been informed by people who have tried to obtain public halls for meetings of the Labour group, or the Independent group ot those who think along our lines, that it is impossible to hire a hall in Toronto on account of the intimidation of the police force of that city. When I spoke there not long ago in the Labour Temple, I was told that before they held the meeting they attempted to get a bigger hall than the Labour Temple, but they were not able to get it for the very reasons I have mentioned.

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Is the city of Toronto
not the holy city of modern times?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I do not know. I know of
only one city where I can see the holy cross lit lip in the evening, and that is the good city of Montreal.
We have, however, found the same form of intimidation taking place in other cities. I wish to say a word or two in reference to the bill itself. I do not know whether the bill as drafted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will altogether meet the situation. It is quite possible that in spite of what is stated in the bill, the police commission of any city may still have the power to prevent a meeting from taking place. I contend that no police officer or commission should have the right to prevent the holding of a meeting which is in its intent peaceful, which is called for the purpose of discussing public questions. This is what has happened in Toronto and possibly in other cities. I understand, although I have not the actual wording before me, that there is some difference between the wording of our criminal code and that of Great Britain in reference to unlawful assemblies. In our code there are certain words which give power to the authorities to prevent meetings from being held [DOT] if those authorities in their own minds believe such meetings will likely lead to breach of the peace.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
British tradition
has always held to the right, of free speech.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
The British tradition of
free speech is well known to every hon. member. I was referring to the law in Great Britain and the law in this country. There is some difference in the wording in our law as compared with that of Great Britain. I think, however, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be an improvement on what we have at the present time. It may to a certain extent take away from the police some of the powers which they have been using in the way of preventing the free expression of thought in Toronto as well as in other parts of Canada. For that reason I wish to support the bill as introduced by my colleague.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: NATURE OP SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I really did not intend to speak on
this question, but I feel that the reputation of Toronto is at stake and I thought as the Toronto representation on this side is numerically small, hon. members opposite would rise to the occasion and defend the fair name of that city. I understand the hon.
member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) did cany out that duty fairly well the last time the bill was before the house.
In the first place I should like to make this general observation that so far as the internal administration of the police department is concerned, we have in Toronto a very efficient chief of police. Crime is at its lowest ebb in Toronto, and that city is no haven of refuge for any criminal. A great deal of the credit for this is due to the chief of police, and to the fact that there is a very efficient board of police commissioners. I do think, however, in all seriousness that the chief of police and the police commission made a very serious error on the question of free speech, in the first place in assuming that the communists in Toronto are a considerable force. I recall speaking to one of the communists before the election, and he told me that the communist party, which consists of about seven individuals, more or less, could not have got the same amount of publicity that they got by reason of the actions of the Toronto police if they had paid thousands of dollars for it. I really believe that the chief of police and the police commission of Toronto are not in touch with the feelings of the great mass of the people on this question. May I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not a communist myself, although perhaps communism as an economic theory may be a proper subject for- debate even in this house. Certainly I am not in favour of the adoption of methods of force to advance any theory. I want to assure the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis), who has cited some correspondence that passed between the chief electoral officer and the communist candidate in Toronto West Centre, who obtained two hundred odd votes in the last election, that I spoke in the same manner as the hon. member himself tried to speak. I attended different meetings and the police never tried to stop me from speaking in the last campaign, nor do I think they tried to stop the gentleman who represented the communist party when he was discussing questions of policy or the economic theories that he held. Only when he attempted to abuse and slander the police force of Toronto was he stopped, and I think rightly stopped, by the police.
The police commission, I think, also made a very serious error in adopting a policy of intimidating the owners of various halls and public buildings. The fact is-I must admit it even if I do come from Toronto-that there is difficulty in renting a hall for any man who wants to express ideas in Toronto that are not shared by the majority of the

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
people of that city-ideas that may be considered advanced or radical. I know that the answer of the police is that the owners of the halls are free to rent their halls if they like, but the difficulty is that the chief of police sends around his emissaries to warn the owners that if they do not refrain from renting the hall to men who the police think will advance such ideas, the licence for the coming year will not be renewed, and I presume it is only human nature for any owner of a hall not to rent it after a diplomatic and tactful hint of that kind from the police.
I think that the city of Toronto has got an unenviable reputation by reason of the actions of the police in this matter during the last year or eighteen months. I do not think that the amendment offered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will cure the situation at all. As a matter of fact the first part of this amendment, that "nothing in this section shall restrict or interfere with the right of all persons peacefully to assemble for the purpose of discussing or hearing any discussion upon any matter of public interest" is the law now. Anyone in Toronto can discuss any matter of public interest if he keeps within the law. Of course the difficulty that is created by the authorities in Toronto is due to their interpretation of what is within the law; in other words, the police authorities assume that because a person is notorious as a radical or holds advanced ideas, anything he might say will not be within the law; and that is where the trouble comes in. But under the law as it stands now, any matter of public interest can be discussed in this country, including the city of Toronto.
The rest of the section, which leaves it to "firm and reasonable persons" to decide what is likely to cause an immediate breach of the peace is a rather curious piece of proposed legislation, in my humble opinion because, in the first place, a "firm and reasonable person," if there be such, is not defined, and before this firm and reasonable person will be able to define what is likely to cause an immediate breach of the peace the breach will be committed, and then there will be no need for any definition. I really believe that the amendment offered will not cure the situation at all.
I think that the fault lay entirely with our police commission, and that the time is soon commg when the entire functions of the police commission will perhaps have to be changed. The personnel of the police commission is changing or soon will change, and with that change I think that the police force of the city of Toronto, including the chief of police, will assume a reasonable attitude and frame

of mind on this question. I do not think that there is anything wrong with the law as it stands, so far as even the city of Toronto is concerned. I believe that the police force in Toronto misinterpreted the law with the result that a handful of communists received a lot of publicity, and with the further result that a great number of people such as the hon. gentlemen in the group to my left were refused permission to speak in the city. I do not know whether that was harmful to the country or not, considering the number of speeches that I have heard in this house from the group to my left. I do want to say, however, that the gentlemen in the corner to my left certainly have no monopoly on political morality or political integrity or freedom of speech. It is unfortunate that some of these gentlemen came to Toronto and could not get a hall to speak in, but I want to assure them, in conclusion, that so far as the city of Toronto is concerned the majority of our people still believe in freedom of speech and still practise freedom of speech, and the time is soon coming when our police will assume a fair and reasonable attitude on this question.

speechtext:
It appears from the discussion we have had on this bill that it is altogether misnamed. It is not an act to amend the criminal code regarding unlawful assemblies at large, but merely an act to amend the criminal code regarding unlawful assemblies in Toronto, and therefore I think that if the hon. gentlemen in the corner want to achieve their purpose they should amend the proposed subsection 4 by adding words which will make it read thus:
Nothing in this section shall restrict or interfere with the right of all persons peacefully to assemble in Toronto for the purpose of discussing or hearing any discussion.
The latter part of the subsection should be amended to read as follows:
Such persons when so assembled in Toronto shall not become an unlawful assembly unless firm and reasonable persons from outside Toronto decide otherwise.
Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not rise to abuse the good city of Toronto, but rather to say a word in its favour, which is very unusual for a Liberal member, especially one coming from the province of Quebec. I may say, and this will be no news to many hon. members, that communist assemblies or meetings have also been prohibited in Montreal because in the past they have become unruly. Meetings were prevented because the speeches delivered had in such a way excited the audience that a veri-

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
table riot resulted. The speech had to be stopped or harm might have resulted. The trouble I find in the proposed legislation is that it is not so muoh a piece of legislation as a literary opinion on the subject of free speech. The bill is very vague in its terms. For instance, who is to decide when persons are peacefully assembled for the purpose of discussing any matter? Many people who appear to be peaceful at eight o'clock are not so peaceful at ten or half past ten. Such communistic speakers as any hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) will rise and, in the most polished language to which one could listen, -Will make a speech which would lead one to believe that they were advocating peace, but if one listened for an hour or so he would find that the remarks had taken a different trend. I submit therefore, that if the hon. member has it in mind to promote the cause of free speech, he does not help it by the proposed section. Its terms are so vague that it seems to me still to leave to the discretion of the police the determination of the question whether or not an assembly is peaceful.
Then the expression is used: "in the opinion of firm and reasonable persons." In my opinion the wording should be more precise. By "firm and reasonable persons" does the hon. member refer to members of the Progressive party? Or does he refer to members of parties representing other sections of our population? In any case I repeat that discretion is left to that person to decide whether a meeting should or should not take place.
Certainly I stand for free speech, and on occasions when I am ruled against by Mr. Speaker, and more often by Mr. Deputy Speaker, I feel that nobody should interfere with any speech. At the same time I know from experience in the city of Montreal that some of the meetings which have been stopped should never have been started. I speak not necessarily from a communistic standpoint but from the standpoint of peace and the avoiding of trouble. I am afraid if this bill passes it will do nothing to alter present conditions. Because of the vagueness of its terms the question whether or not a meeting is peaceful, in the opinion of "firm and reasonable persons", is still left to the discretion of some person in authority. These are matters which cannot be determined by statute, but will always reside within the discretion of those charged with the maintenance of law and order not, only in the city of Toronto but in every city of the Dominion.
