maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was quoting from a letter sent by the city of Vancouver to the Minister of Labour for British Columbia. This letter was addressed to the Minister of Labour, Hon. W. A. McKenzie, and shows the very serious situation in regard to unemployment in the city of Vancouver. It says:
To meet these cases there are no funds provided at present from any source, and as explained to your committee, the city's financial situation will not allow Vancouver to carry fMr. Jacobs.l
this burden. In fact, it will be most difficult for the city to carry on its ordinary relief to the indigent sick and aged. These facts constitute a situation most grave and serions. During the past winter the city has carried some thousands of unemployed who have drifted into Vancouver from other parts of Canada and British Columbia.
Then he goes on to say:
The council trust that the governments will realize the most serious nature of the situation which now exists, and of the inability of the of the city to adequately cope with it, even on the present basis. The situation will be greatly aggravated upon the exhaustion of the government direct relief fund, about April 24. It is recognized that the problem is national in extent, and also that industry can be stimulated and encouraged by the Dominion and provincial governments only. It is therefore urged that these bodies establish immediate and effective means to deal with the situation as outlined herein.
This communication asks the provincial and federal governments to call a conference to discuss the unemployment situation throughout Canada, and it is dated March 31 of this year.- I also have here a report from the relief officer to the relief committee under date of May 9, 1931, in which the following appears:
I regret to have to place before you the continued serious condition of unemployment in this city. In place of the usual seasonal improvement during March there appears to have been an actual decrease in the number of workers employed in the city during the month. . . .
These conditions were reflected in the figures and expenditures of the relief department. Since April 1st the married unemployed eases have increased by 269, and now total 1,346, a number larger than any shown during the past winter.
I ask hon. members of the house and of the government to take particular notice of this statement, that on April 1st the number of married unemployed on direct relief was 1,346, a larger number than any shown during the past winter. This was at a time when we were told conditions were improving, and when in the usual course of events we would have expected them to improve. The report continues:
The aged and handicapped have also had greater difficulty in finding light and occasional work, and in obtaining assistance from their relatives. This fact has increased the number of people on general relief.
That is the general tendency during a long period of unemployment with the reduced wages now in effect in almost every industry and with the part time work, with the employees dividing up their work in order that more people may be kept employed, the workers are becoming increasingly impoverished

Unemployment

Mr. Heaps
and it is more difficult to lend assistance to others who may be more unfortunate. I quote further:
The present situation shows that the council's forecast was only too correct. The city's inability to cope with the situation is even more pronounced to-day than on March 28th.
I would therefore recommend that the strongest possible representations be made in order to convince the governments of the need for prompt and effective action.
Last September, immediately after the general election, the government called a special session of parliament to deal with the situation, thus fulfilling a promise given during the election. At that session the 1930 Unemployment Relief Act was passed. There was some criticism of the way the money was expended under that act, but at this time I do not wish to offer any criticism of that kind. I believe the government, considering the short time at their disposal to formulate a policy, did the very best they possibly could under the circumstances, and I think they should receive-as I believe they have received-due credit for what they did. Now, however, we are facing a situation which is even more serious than that we were facing last September, and the government now have had considerable time to formulate a better policy to take care of unemployment. If something is not done in the very near future, then I feel not only that criticism will be in order but that we should be negligent in our duty if we refrained from offering it.
In connection with the 1930 unemployment relief fund, however, and the way it has affected and further complicated the situation, I should like to quote from a telegram I received from the Vancouver civic employees' union. This is a union of the outside workers of Vancouver, who were engaged in the work on which this money was spent. The telegram is addressed to myself, and is as follows:
I am instructed to advise you of the following resolution passed by the largest meeting of civic employees ever held in Vancouver:
Whereas the operation of the Unemployment Relief Act of 1930 has resulted in a large number of permanent civic employees being laid off on account of their work having been done by relief labour under the terms of the aforementioned act, which called upon the municipality to match dollar for dollar: and
Whereas many more will be laid off this summer as a direct result of said act, the money previously provided to keep them employed having been used for relief;
Be it resolved that this union strongly condemn this act and request you to bring the results as they apply to us to the notice of the government and if possible read this wire
in the house, and also to request that relief moneys in the future be provided by the government on the basis of the number of unemployed in each locality and not on the basis of their ability to match dollar for dollar.
The position in which the permanent employees of the city of Vancouver find themselves at the present moment is that the funds usually provided to keep men employed during the year have been used in order to meet the funds granted by this government, and therefore these men are no longer employed. So the city not only has the ordinary unemployed "o look after, but in addition there are six or seven hundred of their permanent staff for whom provision must be made.
I would urge upon the government, therefore, that they give immediate and serious consideration at least to the calling of a conference, if they have not something better with which to meet the situation, in order that we may have a full understanding of the seriousness of the unemployment conditions throughout this Dominion, and make provision for meeting them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
had hoped that some member of the government would rise in his place and explain to the house and the country what action the government have in mind to cope with the very serious unemployment situation which prevails at the present time. There is no doubt whatever that even during these summer months there exists in Canada an unemployment situation the like of which I have never known at this time of year. Consequently there is need for immediate action of some kind on the part of the government, first of all to allow the municipalities to do something, to acquaint the provincial governments with any contemplated action, and also to give at least some hope to the thousands of men and women who find themselves out of work.
Already some hon. members who have spoken have dealt with the unemployment situation in their own localities, and perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might give a picture of conditions as they existed in Winnipeg just a few weeks ago. It was shown according to the table I have under my hand, published by a committee of citizens, that in the greater Winnipeg area there were 18,893 persons out of work. These with their families represented a total of 56,682 people. In other words, probably more than twenty per cent of the total population of the greater Winnipeg area is out of work, and I believe most of them
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

are also in want. Coming down to what are the prospects, this committee reports as follows:
Other than the jobs which will be undertaken as relief projects, there is no prospect of employment increase in sight. The jobs which will be started as soon as weather permits will employ in suburban municipalities . adjacent to Winnipeg, in the neighbourhood of 225 men.
The report proceeds:
The Winnipeg Citizens Committee on Unemployment, under the chairmanship of Mr. H. B. Shaw', addressed a letter to prominent persons at country points, enquiring as to the possibility of absorbing in agricultural pursuits the surplus labour in Winnipeg. Replies received were very pessimistic, and were generally to the effect that farmers would not be hiring men this season because of the general depression in the agricultural field, that farmers were satisfied that they would be unable to pay the wages of any men employed, and consequently that any crops put in would be put in by the farmer and his family.
Further on in the same report I find the following observation:
The committee has written a letter to every lumber firm that ordinarily operates in this vicinity, enquiring as to the employment prospects for the winter 1931-32, and the replies received would indicate that fewer men will be employed during the coming winter than were [DOT]employed during the past winter. In other words, instead of eight or ten thousand men it may be expected that there will be fewer than eight hundred men taken from Winnipeg's surplus labour market.
The report is signed by H. B. Shaw, chairman, Winnipeg citizens' committee on unemployment; by Ralph Maybank, chairman, joint unemployment committee, city of Winnipeg; and by A. MaeNamara, assistant deputy minister, and administrator of unemployment relief in Manitoba.
Only this morning I received a letter from the mayor of the city of Brandon, imploring me to do what I possibly could to assist him to obtain further relief for his city, and pointing out that there is a very serious unemployment situation in Brandon, and that they are in a position where they have great difficulty in coping with the large number of men out of work. He points out that the little work being carried out was being done by machinery and that very few men were actually employed.
It was pointed out in the report published by the Department of Labour that during the past winter, as a result of the special Unemployment Relief Act of 1930, 228,351 persons were given employment. It was also pointed out that almost 200,000 persons were in receipt of direct relief as a result of the operations of the act. My own computations on the

figures published by the Labour department would indicate that during the past winter approximately 350,000 people were given assistance either through work or directly in the way of food, clothing and shelter. That will give the house some indication of the seriousness of the unemployment situation which prevails throughout the Dominion.
I do not think the government will for a moment say that they have not got a responsibility in this matter. I was rather surprised when yesterday I heard the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gordon) who represents in this house the Minister of Labour, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr Neill) say that if the municipality and then the province could not deal with the situation the federal government would take action I had thought that by this time the federal government fully realized their responsibility and were prepared to take the initiative in coping with the existing situation. I appreciate the great difficulty that the government may have in attempting to find work for all those who are unemployed at the present time. I think it is well nigh impossible for the federal government and the provincial governments to provide anything like permanent employment for the vast numbers of the unemployed. But at the same time I am very anxious that the government let it be known what they intend to do in regard to the question, so that, as I said before, the unemployed, the municipalities and the provinces will at least know what is going to be done in the very near future.
I do not wish to enter into any long discussion as to why we have this unemployment situation. There is no doubt opportunities will present themselves as the session * progresses to discuss it from that particular angle. However, we have been asked by hon. gentlemen opposite on so many occasions: What have we to suggest by way of coping with the existing difficulties? May I say to those hon. gentlemen that first of all the government have to admit one thing, that they have no remedies themselves for the unemployment problem. The moment we have that admission that these so-called remedies of tariff adjustments are no remedies at all, we are prepared to deal with the question and offer our suggestions.
I should like to point out that what we are suffering from to-day is not a lack of production. In fact according to government figures during the period from 1920 to 1928 individual productivity in the Dominion increased by approximately 53 per cent. Therefore if we are to find any remedies we have to go

<S upply-A gric ult ure-Dairy in g
outside the remedies already suggested and find some other means of dealing with the problem. To-day we are living in an age of high production and comparatively low consumption, and in some way we have to relate our purchasing power-in other words our ability to consume-to out productive capacity. Whilst we have learned to produce in superabundance, there has been no opportunity given to the workers to allow them to consume the goods which they themselves have produced.
As I said a few minutes ago, I had hoped that on this occasion the acting Minister of Labour or some other member of the government would have risen in his place and stated to the house and to the country at large what is proposed to cope with the situation. I know it may be said to us that we are a little impatient. If we of the Labour group in this house and others are a little impatient in attempting to find out what the government intend to do to cope with the unemployment situation, our only answer would be to the effect that to-day there are hundreds of thousands of people walking our streets, not knowing where they can obtain work or other relief or where their next meal is coming from. It was pointed out by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) a few moments ago when discussing another question, that only this morning in Winnipeg 1,500 men went down to try to obtain work where only 100 were wanted. Imagine the natural resentment of those people when they found a piece of modern machinery doing the work that ordinarily takes several hundred people to perform. The disappointment resulted in a little riot. No one wants to see these riots occur, but it is difficult to say what a desperate person will do when in a desperate situation.
In view of these circumstances I do not think we are asking anything unreasonable when we request the acting Minister of Labour or any other -hon. member of the government to rise in his place and state to the unemployed people of this country, men who are good citizens and who have wives and children depending upon them, men who do not know what the morrow is going to bring forth, the intentions of the government.
Many of the municipalities are not in a position to provide work out of their own resources. That is another problem which the federal government will have to consider and consider very seriously. Many municipalities are almost on the verge of bankruptcy; they have very- limited borrowing powers and very limited sources of revenue, and when we ask them to assume one-third of the cost
of relief work in many instances we are putting a burden upon them which it is almost impossible for them to bear. I hope that in any proposal which the government submit to this house they do not ask the municipalities, and particulary those of western Canada, to assume one-third of the cost of relief work, the other two-thirds to be assumed by the provinces and by the federal government. This government should assume from 50 to 66J per cent of the cost, and unless something of that nature is done I have grave doubts as to whether the municipalities will be in a position to undertake any active relief work. I sincerely hope that before this debate is concluded some member of the government will rise in his place and state what is the attitude of the government towards this question, which I believe to be the most important question to be faced by parliament.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before we
enter into a discussion of the details of these estimates I would like to have an opportunity of saying a few words in a general way, particularly as to the point of view from which we are to discuss these estimates. It will be recalled that on a former occasion, speaking to an amendment to the motion that the house go into supply. I quoted from a speech the Prime Minister had made at Woodstock in which he promised to put all the collective power of the government behind agriculture. It is from that point of view that I wish to discuss these estimates, to see just how far they fulfil that promise. In replying to me the Prime Minister referred to these estimates, and if I may be permitted, I will quote his remarks, as follows:
What struck me as passing strange was that the hon. member for Lisgar should complain that someone in England was no longer to be continued in his position, although the estimates for agriculture contain a much larger sum than had been used heretofore for the very purposes he mentioned. Did he look at the estimates himself? Did he see what the provisions are for agriculture? Did he compare them with last year or the year before? Did he see evidences of the very earnest desire of the minister to put into effect the policy he advocates?

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
Not only by implication but by direct statement the Prime Minister gave the house to understand that these estimates represented the implementing of the promises he had made to put the collective powers of the government behind agriculture.
I want to remind the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) that it is from that point of view that we intend to-night to discuss the question whether or not these estimates fulfil the promises made by the Prime Minister. That is what we are interested in. We are not interested in the educational qualifications or the former political affiliations of the minister, although we are somewhat interested in his present political affiliations. W'hen the minister accepted the invitation of the Prime Minister to enter his cabinet he thereby accepted responsibility for the fulfilling of the pledges .made by the Prime Minister during the election. If he has given any attention to the development of constitutional government in British countries he will know that under our doctrine of cabinet solidarity the ministers are individually and collectively responsible for the policies of the government. It is the consideration of that point of view that I want to urge upon the committee.
I should like to glance briefly at the estimates in general before we discuss them in detail. The Prime Minister pointed out that the increase in these estimates amounted to $414,564.64. There are seventeen items, six of which show increases and five of which show decreases. The largest increases are shown in the following items: experimental farms, an increase of $175,000; assistance to fairs and exhibitions, including the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair, an increase of $650,000; grant to the executive committee of the World's. Grain Congress, an increase of $100,000. The increase in these three items totals $925,000, and yet the net increase in all the items amounts to only $414,564.64, showing that in some of the other important items there must be a considerable decrease. It will be a matter of interest to the committee if in the discussion of these estimates in detail the Minister of Agriculture can Show us what has been done to implement the promise made by the Prime Minister in his speech at Woodstock that he would put the collective power of the government behind agriculture. That is all I wish to say at the moment. No doubt as the various estimates come before the committee, I shall have further remarks to make.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I notice in this item No. 107 a $5,000 grant to the National Dairy Council. I am opposed to that grant. The National Dairy Council, I understand, was formed some years ago for the purpose of assisting dairy farmers on the road to prosperity. The original conception may have been all right, but the association was unfortunate in the choice of its officers. The direction of its affairs fell into the hands of men who were so barren of original ideas as to how to help the dairy farmer that they could think of nothing other than to persuade him to ask the government for higher duties on his products. So the National Dairy Council became nothing but an organization to propagate Tory doctrines, to lead the farmer to believe that in some way a higher duty on butter or other dairy products would be of benefit to him. They so far succeeded in their propaganda that they persuaded many farmers last summer to support the present government. They have been successful in getting from the present government the higher duties on dairy products; in fact they have got twice as much as they asked for. Now we know the result; now the farmer realizes that he has been led up a blind alley, that he has been deceived by this association which promised him better things if he would but vote for the Tory party and platform.
I am opposed on principle to the use of money out of the public treasury for the carrying on of political propaganda, I care not what party or policy it supports. The men who have been leaders of the National Dairy Council and, through that council, leaders of the farmers' movement, have proved themselves to be blind leaders of the blind. They are no longer worthy of the confidence of the farmers and we have no right to grant public money to them to carry on their propaganda. Therefore I move that the item be reduced by $5,000, being the amount of a grant to the National Dairy Council.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I think in going over these estimates hon. members will realize that except in respect to two or three particular lines I have made as few changes as possible from the estimates of other years. I felt that those who had been in office for a number of years would be in a better position, except where I had very definite reasons for making a change, to decide how money should be expended, than I would be with only a few months' experience. For years, I understand, this vote of $5,000 has been given to the

National Dairy Council in the belief that from the way it is constituted it was representative of the dairy interests and of the distributors. I can assure the hon, member who has just spoken that ait the expiration of this financial year, if I do not feel that the National Dairy Council contributes something really worth while to the dairy industry, I shall be the first to see that this vote is left out. At the present time, however, in view of the statement I have made and the reasons I have for leaving it in, I feel that ithe vote should remain as it is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am discussing the item more closely than the hon. member ever discussed an item in his life. Last winter in Essex and Kent counties we sold 320.000 bags of onions, due to the fact that the National Dairy Council of Canada recommended to the government-

The point of
order is that the hon. member is not discussing the item before us.

I understand the hon.
member for South Essex is connecting his onions with the National Dairy Council. Otherwise he would not be in order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Since I have been in the house I have never seen the hon. member for South Huron in order. I realize it is my duty as *the sitting member for Essex county to say to the Minister of Agriculture that the onion growers of Essex and Kent counties appreciate this S5,000 expenditure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There seems to be a dispute
as to what this item covers. Will the minister tell us what the item of S295.000 was spent for last year? Then we shall find out whether the hon. member for South Essex or the hon. member for South Huron is in order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some of this vote will be spent in the administration of the branch, and the greater part of it in the payment of inspectors in different parts of the country, both butter inspectors and cheese inspectors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Any onion inspectors?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some of it will be spent on research work in the dairy industry, and some will be spent on advertising to encourage people in the use of milk and butter and dairy products in various forms.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much money was spent in the province of Quebec for the cheese and butter inspectors, and where are they located?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the city of Montreal we have seventeen dairy produce graders, and two in the province of Quebec otheT than Montreal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

In Montreal one
receives $3,240, and there are fifteen at $2,760, and one grade 2 inspector at $2,580. The
