travelling expenses for the Montreal officials amount to $2,000. For the, province of Quebec other than Montreal we have one dairy produce grader, grade 2, at $2,760, another at S2,520, and travelling expenses SKI.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have any changes been made in this staff since the month of August last?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not that I know of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same men are still there?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So far as I know.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister has said that as few changes were made as possible, and he also stated in answer to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay that the salaries of the dairy produce graders are included in this vote of $295,000. In this connection I should like to invite the attention of the committee to an article that appeared in all the western papers in the form of a despatch from Ottawa dated May 8th last, dealing with the agricultural policy of this government. I think there will be no more propitious time than the present to quote from this article. I shall not read it all, because in the beginning it deals principally with the, speech that was made by the Minister of Agriculture some time ago in this house. It says in part: Ottawa, Ont., May 8.-Mr. Weir is of a nervous temperament and his friends were anxious over his first effort to address parliament. For weeks he had been subjected to sniping and the most cowardly attacks from such members as Donnelly of Willow Bunch. Vallance of North Battleford and Young of Weyburn, culminating in an offensive attack by Hon. W. R. Motherwell.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps hon. gentlemen will say "hear, hear," before I get through. The article continues:
The former Minister of Agriculture never was noted for refinement, but in his references to Mr. Weir he was more coarse than ever before in methods and manners.
The new Minister of Agriculture caught the ear of the house from the start. He showed no mercy for Premier King or Mr. Motherwell or Saskatchewan Liberals. Mr. Weir was not only justified in his' attack through the attitude of previous Liberal speakers, but he has a task as great almost as the Prime Minister's.
Perhaps hon. gentlemen will say, "hear, hear," now:
There never has been a department in Ottawa so incompetent, in such a state of inefficiency and disorganization as agriculture when W. R. Motherwell left it. The department was and still is inefficiently manned, permeated with intrigue, jealousies and incompetence. Mr. Motherwell gave no thought to agriculture. 
I read that for the benefit of the farmers of Canada.
He was a political minister. When exports fell off, he said in excuse the people at home were eating more. There was no attempt to grade beef, butter or similar products for export.
Then why this item of $295,000? I should like the minister to explain that. The. article continues:
It was under these conditions that Mr. W7eir took office. He had scarcely a competent official, and many were disloyal to him. He did not tell the whole story last night, but on his estimates parliament will receive further information on the decrepit department left by Mr. Motherwell.
We want to receive that information tonight. It goes on:
There will also be a further elaboration on Mr. Weir's new departures in agricultural production and marketing.
I have glanced through these estimates and I see no very radical changes from last year. I hope before the Minister of Agriculture gets through, and I do not suppose he will get through to-night, that he will either confirm or refute these statements that have permeated the west regarding the condition of the - Department of Agriculture, because those of us who are deeply interested in agriculture do not believe they are true. I know a great many of the officials of the department and have met them on various committees, and I know that they are very competent and very efficient. I think they need more in the way of commendation than condemnation. I do not think it is fair either to the Minister of Agriculture or to his officials that these statements should be allowed to go out all over Canada unrefuted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Weyburn has made the same remarks regarding the vote for the National Dairy Council as he did last year, and consequently is quite consistent in his attitude. If I am to be consistent with my attitude of that day I must oppose my hon. friend from Weyburn.
I find myself in the first round favouring the attitude of the minister that this is a good vote, and so long as the National Dairy Council performs as good service as it has done in the past on behalf of dairying it will receive my support.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
I would ask the minister if the total of $9.515,343.44, which appears in the column for 1930-31, includes the supplementaries voted early in the session.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As a rule the supplementaries that are passed at the beginning of the session are added to the old vote of last year because the expenditure was incurred last year. I think the minister is wrong; perhaps he may not have understood my question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman means the supplementaries that were put through at the beginning of this session-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand that
they are not included.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They should be included. In that case there would be a less rote this year than last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A greater vote. The supplementary estimates voted at the beginning of this session, I am Informed, are in addition to this.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But they were spent last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are in addition to what is here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In addition to this
$9,515,343.44?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But that money was spent last year and consequently the vote for this year is just about $100,000 less than that of last year. Perhaps the hon. member has not done justice to himself. Undoubtedly his deputy knows what I am getting at. In the supplementary estimates passed at the beginning of each session to take care of expenditures already incurred, as in the case of the health of animals branch, for which there was an appropriation of $300,000, such sums are invariably added to the vote of the year in which the moneys were spent. However we will let the matter stand at present.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the hon.
member is right. The supplementary vote at the beginning of this session is not included in the amount set out in the main estimates, so that as stated by the hon. member it will be considered as an expenditure of last year. The vote for last year will therefore be higher than it appears on the information before us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is what
I am trying to say. My hon. friend has produced an estimate, then, which is smaller than that of last year, rather than greater, as would appear from the main estimates. I think my hon. friend is wrong and has done himself an injustice. In order that he may settle the matter with his deputy I will not press it further at this time.
There is another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members. During the late election campaign the butter question was discussed everywhere, and to my mind the time has arrived for a review of the situation concerning that particular commodity. I shall not, however, go into the matter very extensively to-night. Hon. members 'opposite led the people to believe that because of the action of the Liberal government the dairy industry was on the toboggan. What is the. proper yardstick by which to measure a dairy industry? Is it the amount of blitter made, or the amount of cheese made? Is it any one of fifteen or twenty other dairy products? No; I suggest we should use the yardstick of the number of pounds of milk produced in a given year. To my mind that is the only proper measurement. It does not matter what the farmer converts the milk into. He may use it to produce any commodity he wishes, or any form which he can derive the greatest amount of money. I wonder if the minister has the data concerning the number of pounds of milk produced. If he has not, I may tell him that I have the figures before me. For the information of hon. members I shall give the committee a general survey of the milk production from 1922 to the present. I shall not attempt to be absolutely accurate, but will merely give the round figures. In 1922 nearly ten billions pounds of milk were produced from the dairy cows of Canada. In 1923, eleven billion pounds were produced; in 1924, twelve billion; in 1925, twelve billion, five hundred million; in 1926, thirteen billion; in 1927, fourteen billion; in 1928. fourteen billion; in 1929, fourteen billion. In the last two years there was a slight falling off in production, amounting to only a few million pounds. These figures show an increase of over four billion pounds or 40 per cent in the production of milk in Canada during the nine years of Liberal administration. That is a different story from the one told by hon. members opposite in the province of British Columbia and throughout the maritimes in the election campaign.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And in Quebec.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The people would not listen to our story; we could not get it across. My hon. friends opposite were in the field twelve months ahead of us and they 'had been successful in filling the minds of the public with their views in the matter. At this date, after the election everybody seems to be satisfied with the result,-something which to my mind is most extraordinary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friends on this side of the house are quite satisfied, but I am not sure that my hon. friends opposite are satisfied. It would be quite natural, of course, if they were. The figures I have placed on record represent a 40 per cent increase in the production of milk in Canada. I wonder if the minister's figures agree with mine in this respect, because if they do the talk during the election campaign goes up the flue-there is nothing to it. Even in connection with butter the production became greater.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it a fact that about the year 1029 the figures concerning the production of milk in Canada were changed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not under examination, but if my hon. friend wishes to put me in-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have asked whether the figures Showing the total production of milk in Canada for the years 1927, 1928 and 1929 were changed just before the last election in order to produce the figures now placed on Hansard by the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figures I have quoted are official and are those of the dairy branch based upon elaborate and expensive information supplied by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I think if the deputy minister has his figures before him he will find they tally with those I have given. Of course I expected hon. members to have an alibi, but I had expected a better one than that which has been given by the hon. member for South Hastings.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us have the correct figures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let the minister answer for himself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is some doubt in the minds of hon. members on the other side concerning the figures given by the hon. member for Melville. I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture give us the figures.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is an amendment before the committee, does the. committee wish to dispose of it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We ought to have a statement from the minister so that we may find out whether the figures placed on record by the hon. member for Melville are correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have now before us a statement of the figures showing the production of milk for the years mentioned. I do not think the effect of legislation by the present government to assist the dairy industry will be questioned, so far as butter is concerned, by any hon. member on either side. Had it not been for the tariff we placed on butter what would have been the effect on receipts of the dairy farmers of Canada?
Mr. TOTZKE; What difference would it have made?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What effect did it have?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At the time the present government -came into power the prices of butter in Canada and the United States, London and Australia, were these: In Canada, 28 to 28.25 cents per pound; in the United States, 35.25 to 35.50 cents per pound.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What date is that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The beginning of
August.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that the wholesale price?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, obtained from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and the prices are on the same basis for each country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At what points in Canada were those prices quoted?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the minister quoting the Montreal price or the New York price?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The information we have is the average price of butter as recognized by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The average for all the
countries?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the present government came into power the price in Canada was 28 to 28.25 cents per pound. At the same time the price of butter in the United States was 35.25 to 35.50 cents per pound, and in London, 28.64 to 29.08. On March 17, 1981, the price of butter in Canada was higher than the price in the United States and six cents higher than Australian butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are the figures?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On March 17, 1931, the price of butter in Canada was 31 cents a pound, and in the United States, 29'75; Australian butter in London, 25-6 to 25-82. It was estimated, from the number of pounds of butter produced in Canada, having regard to the difference between this price and the price that would have been paid on the same basis, that this has put into the pockets of the farmers of Canada 82,000,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is the price in Canada
to-day?
Mr: WEIR (Melfort):	No one regrets
more than I do the rapid drop in the price of butter during a period of ten days, but the price of butter in Canada at the present time, due largely to some butter which is being shipped out-there are over 250,000 pounds on the ocean going to the old country-has risen from the low price on May 12 of 18-5 to 18-75 to a price to-day of 21 to 21-25, and the market is the firmest it has been since before the slide we all regret, which occurred some time ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the minister
tell the committee how long ago it was that the price of butter for export was as low as it is now? Was ;t before the war, or before the flood, or when was it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The effect on the
price of butter of the action of this government can be fairly arrived at only by a comparison with other countries on a London parity of the price of butter when we came into power and the price at the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I agree with the
hon. gentleman to some extent-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would
like the floor for a moment; the hon. member for Melville cannot monopolize the discussion. I was on my feet first, and I claim the floor. I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if Canada is not to-day on an export basis for the first time in two years. Is it not also a fact that we did not make enough
butter to satisfy our own domestic requirements before this government came into power, and that under the late Minister of Agriculture we were eating Australian butter right up here in the parliamentary restaurant?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is because people
cannot buy the butter that we are on the export basis.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At page 1361 of Hansard for this session I find that the Minister of Agriculture said:
I am told by the dairy commissioner and by produce merchants that we have no Canadian butter sufficiently uniform as to grade to permit its being labelled and shipped to the old country as Canadian butter.
I wonder, if we are on an export basis, what has been done in order to get us on that basis. In the past has the butter not been properly graded and labelled? Have our inspectors and commissioners been neglecting their duty? What was wrong that Canada was not previously on this basis? Are we not able to make butter of good enough quality for export, or what?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One of the reasons why the butter is not uniform is the number of very small creameries, where it is almost impossible to get it absolutely uniform because of the size of the creamery. We have an advantage in the west and also in the east in our larger creameries in getting a uniform brand. My statement was this, that the butter as produced in Canada is not sufficiently uniform for a national trade mark of any kind. The butter which is being shipped, I understand, is being selected in Montreal as uniformly as possible, for shipment to the old land.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is the minister
doing to see that it is made uniform? That is what I want to know.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Inspectors are
carrying on the work and trying to encourage the smaller creameries to have their butter conform to the uniform standard we wish to have prevail.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are being told now that we are on an export basis, and that is the reason for the low price of butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the idea, then, of mentioning the fact?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I were a Presbyterian minister I would not talk like that.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My understanding of the
Statement of the minister was that we were on an export basis, which accounted for the low price of butter. All I can say is that when it was proposed to raise the duty on butter, many of us who objected to that step took the position that while it might temporarily benefit the farmer, it could not ultimately do so and that as soon as we got on an export basis we would have to take the export price. The only event out of the ordinary is that the result has come about a little sooner than we anticipated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The farmer who is producing the cream is interested in the price of butter, but he is more interested in the price of butter fat. I have a letter here which I received to-day from my home town, in which my correspondent says that special cream sells for 20 cents at the creamery, and No. 1 churning cream at 16 cents. Based on these figures, he paid 30 cents a pound for creamery butter right where the butter is made. He says the creamery has an overrun of one-fifth, and based on the price of special cream-and all this is not special cream-that makes four cents. Then they charge the merchant five cents profit, and in turn he charges another five cents. This gives the farmer twenty cents as compensation for capital invested in land, buildings, feed, cattle, labour, bringing the cream to town and so on, while the creamery gets approximately nine cents and the merchant five cents, or a total of fourteen cents. If this pound of butter which my correspondent bought had been made from No. 1 cream instead of special cream on a basis of 16 cents per pound I think it would figure out in this way: Considering that one and one-sixth pounds of butter can be made from one pound of butter fat, this man would pay 35 cents for the one and one-sixth pounds of butter made from one pound of butter fat. Of course that would have to include the salt and water put in at the creamery. The farmer would get 16 cents for the pound of butter fat that went into the butter; the local merchant would get a profit of 5 cents, and that would leave 14 cents to the creamery. In other words, there would be a total of 19 cents to the creamery and the retailer, while 16 cents would go to the producer for the pound of butter fat.
The reason I am bringing these figures before the committee to-night is that I may ask the minister whether this vote of $295,000 for dairying can be used in some way to help the farmer get a larger share of what

the people of Canada are paying for their butter. I think that is the real work before our dairy branch at the present time. It does not do the farmer much good to have the price of butter raised-if that were possible-if that increase is not reflected back to him in the price of cream. I should be very glad to have the minister give us some information in regard to this matter and tell us whether there is anything his department could do to see that the price received for butter fat more nearly approximates the price the people of Canada are paying for creamery butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just in confirmation of what the hon. member has said, I may say that I received a letter from one of the members of the Alberta house, a man with some intelligence and some knowledge of the country, who gave me a list of prices of various commodities. This letter was written on May 21. He says that butter fat had just fallen to a new low of 14 cents a pound for No. 1, which is 2 cents lower than the price mentioned. One of the most essential parts of the work that could be done by this branch of the Department of Agriculture would be to see if it is not possible to diminish the spread that exists between the price of butter fat on the one hand and of butter on the other. As has been said, it is not the price of butter that concerns the farmer, for nearly all the butter consumed to-day is made in the creameries; it is the price he receives from the creameries, and it is obvious that at 14 cents a pound for butter fat, even with the low price of feed, he cannot produce it at a profit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The manufacture of butter by creameries is, I take it, a provincial matter. I assume that the figures quoted are for the production of butter from cooperative creameries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister 'a minute ago gave us the prices quoted for butter on May 12 and to-day. Would he be kind enough to give us the corresponding figures for the United States and'the United Kingdom on the same dates?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not those figures here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I point out to the minister that the figures which I quoted refer to prices paid by the Burns Creamery at Nanton, not by a cooperative creamery. It seems to me that the Department of Agriculture might interest itself in such a ques-

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
tion, because after all there is no use increasing the production of butter fat unless the farmer can get a bigger share out of it than he is getting at the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I noticed a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. minister said nobody was more sorry than himself for the drop in butter prices. But he gave the excuse that the price of butter in Canada compares fairly well with the price in other countries, although in reply to a subsequent question from the member for Weyburn he was not able to quote exact figures. May I point out to the minister that his language is hardly consistent with the language of his friends during the last electoral campaign. The fact that he is sorry for the drop in the price of butter does not prevent the price from dropping, and his friends were very definite in their promise that if they were returned to power the price of butter would go up. I am afraid there are people in this country more sorry than the minister for the drop in the price of butter-those who voted for his friends on the strength of their definite promises that the price would go up. My hon. friend says that the butter prices in Canada compare very favourably with those prevailing in other countries. But the Conservative candidates would not admit that contention in July, 1930; they would not admit the least comparison to be made between Canada and other countries as regards practically every question then before the electorate, but particularly on the question of butter prices. I travelled a great deal during the last campaign and was not stopped by a rainstorm like my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. I was able to fulfil all my engagements, and. in the thirty-five or forty counties that I visited I was met by the same question from the Liberal candidates: What are we going to reply to the speeches made by the Conservative candidates, who say most positively that if the Mackenzie King government is defeated and the Hon. Mr. Bennett is put in power butter will sell for 50 or 60 cents a pound in the month of August.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They said so everywhere.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not sure that even
my good friend the Postmaster General did not speak very strongly on the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think he promised that butter would go up in price.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was unknown by the hon. gentleman. .

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend, but I hope that when the electors voted for him they knew him. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will not think we are pressing him too much tonight on tuis item. I may remind him that probably tie main factor that helped the Conservative party in the province of Quebec was the promise so frequently made that if they got into power the price of butter would rise. You will fil'd that the cities of Montreal, St. Hyacinthe, Three Rivers, Hull, Sherbrooke, and Quebec, voted strongly for the Liberal candidates, but the butter argument was very effective in some of the rural ridings. When my hon. friend to-night says that he deeply regrets the drop in the price of butter, I am afraid thar that will not be considered any fulfilment of the promises made by his friends in tie province of Quebec. Certainly if this government has a definite mandate from the electors of the province of Quebec, it is to keep up the price of butter. I know that they cannot do it, but why did they promise what they are not now in a position to carry out?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like, Mr. Chairman, to add a few words to this discussion. We have figures of the comparative prices of butter in the United States and in Canada, and those figures are very significant. Until 1925 our butter compared very favourably with American butter in regard to price, but in 1925, after the Australian treaty came into force, our butter was sold for much less than the price the commodity brought in the United States. So much was this the case that in the first fifteen days of September, 1926, the American farmer was receiving 26 cents a pound more for his butter than the Canadian farmer was receiving; he was getting 55 cents a pound and the Canadian farmer was getting 29 cents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the duty?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can you give us the figures for January, 1930?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The cost of butter in Canada has been comparatively low since the advent of the Australian treaty. The efforts of the ex-Minister of Agriculture to convince members of this house that our milk production had increased is rather far-fetched. The price of butter on account of the importation of the New Zealand commodity-
Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was higher in Canada than in the United States last winter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was lower after the advent of the treaty. During the campaign last July we did not go about this country telling the electors that they were going to get 50 or 60 cents a pound for their butter, at least, not in my section of the country. We told them that we were going to prevent external competition. The dairying industry in Canada was absolutely ruined by the Australian treaty, which was the most iniquitous piece of legislation ever enacted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the industry any better off to-day?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Our prices to-day compare very favourably with the prices obtaining in other countries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not the answer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The cold storage plants in the city of Montreal still contain large quantities of New Zealand butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A couple of million pounds.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much was in storage last year?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fifty million pounds were brought in last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. members may not interrupt the hon. member who has the floor without first asking his permission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a crime that 50,000,000 pounds of foreign butter were brought into this dairying country. Butter prices will not improve until we first get rid of that butter in cold storage, at which time there will be a gradual rise in price although I think it will be some time before we will again see a price of fifty cents per pound.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is not that what you promised at the last election?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The price received by the farmer for his butter, compared with the price he pays for grain, is better than it was last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The price of wheat has gone down more than the price of butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With grain at 30 cents and middlings at 40 cents, it costs the farmer 40 cents per pound to produce butter, but when the price of grain is much cheaper his cost of production is lower. I will have to support the appropriation asked for.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am very much surprised to hear the speech made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi because if there is any hon. member in this house who holds his seat because of butter it is he. I think he is very' ungrateful to the commodity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was very much surprised at the statement of the hon. member for St. James that the farmers had been promised during last summer that they would receive 50 cents per pound for butter. In the industrial section of Canada which I have the honour to represent it was the members of the liberal party who told the mill workers in the town of Cornwall that if the Conservatives were returned to power they would have to pay 50 cents per pound for butter. I have no doubt that if the argument was used there, it was used in the industrial centres of Quebec which, according to -my hon. friend, returned Liberal members. Anyone who has studied the situation must agree with the evidence produced by the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. One of the reasons for the present low price of butter is the fact that there still remain in the storage warehouses of Canada large quantities of New Zealand butter. The present day comparison with foreign prices is more favourable than it has been for the last five or six years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Stormont says that at the last election the price of butter was fixed at 50 cents per pound. I am sorry to report that it has not as yet reached that price.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There seem to be different opinions as to the amount of butter in cold storage, but I have the figures as of March 1, 1930, and March 1, 1931, furnished by the dairy commissioner, Mr. Ruddick. On March 1, 1930, we had in storage 13,087,236 pounds, and on March 1, 1931, 11,272,920 pounds. The statement is made that the amount of New Zealand butter coming in this y'ear has brought the price down but it did not seem to bring it down last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The duty kept the
price up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How much
butter has -come in from Australia and New Zealand since August last? When addressing the house some time ago the hon. minister told us that he had made a verbal agreement with Mr. Moloney of Australia that there was

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
to be no Australian butter released for sale in Canada under 32 cents per pound. Would he tell the committee what has been done with the butter imported from Australia since October last?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In reply to the first allegation, that it was stated at the time of the elections that the price of butter would be increased, I think a fairer interpretation to put on the statement made in that connection would be that we desired the Canadian dairy farmer to be protected against butter which could be produced in other countries at a lower cost. We promised that we would do all in our power to protect him, and we did so. I am informed by a very reliable authority in the butter-making industry that the farmers of Canada would have received during the last winter months at least 10 cents per pound less for their butter had this government not taken the action it did. Another statement made was to the effect that the tariff on butter had increased production, but I think the majority of those in touch with the farming industry in Canada will realize that during the last twelve or eighteen months the main element which tended toward increased production of butter was the cheap coarse grains and the effort which the farmer had to make, to a greater extent than ever before, to increase his income.
In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for South Huron as to the verbal agreement with Australia, I would state that although it was in our power when the treaty with New Zealand was abrogated to put a duty on New Zealand butter, we could not put a higher duty on Australian butter until the treaty with that country had been abrogated, and to do that would have taken some months. Realizing the conditions then existing in Canada, and wishing to give the farmer every protection, we came to the conclusion that the only way that could be done was by a verbal agreement with the Hon. Parker Moloney that pending ratification of the New Zealand treaty no Australian butter would be sold in the Dominion of Canada at less than 32 cents per pound, without a mutual agreement between himself and myself. They lived up to that agreement in a very commendable way, until the price of butter in Montreal, and also in the west, in Vancouver, was cut by something very much in the nature of a butter warfare between various organizations in the west. We thought butter had reached rock bottom, and it was not fair, after Australia had lived up to the agreement as she did, that we shoul not allow her to release her butter on this market.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much butter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the neighbourhood of 10,000 boxes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How can the minister or Mr. Moloney control the price of butter? Is the minister or is Mr. Moloney in the butter business?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are, I hope,
and always shall be in the business of looking after the interests of the dairy farmers of Canada. The hon. gentleman is no doubt aware that in Australia they have an export board than can control the export of butter, and it was by making use of that organization that Mr. Moloney was able to control it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask the minister how he can control the price of butter in Canada or prevent the Australian people from selling butter at any price they like in this country,

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The price of butter exported from Australia is under the Australian export board. They were the people who controlled it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the minister in his statement a moment ago admitted that while he and Mr. Moloney made an agreement, that agreement was broken by somebody and the price of butter was reduced.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that in Montreal last week, butter sold retail for twenty cents a pound?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Australian butter
was not released at less than thirty-two cents a pound until we released the Hon. Parker Moloney and the Australian government from their agreement with us. They controlled the butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did the minister do that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because we felt
that they had kept their agreement honourably prior to that time, and butter had reached bottom price.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But we were exporting
Canadian butter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister has not
answered my question. What I should like to know is this:	If we made an agreement
with Mr. Moloney of Australia to keep butter at thirty-two cents, why did he release Mr. Moloney from his agreement, or why did the price decrease?
Suppl y-A gricult ure-Dairying

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot answer the question any better than I have done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Of course the minister cannot; that is the trouble.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall repeat the
answer I gave before. The verbal agreement made with the Hon. Parker Moloney was this: that they would not release Australian butter in Canada at less than thirty-two cents a pound except by mutual agreement, as long as we felt that to do so would injure the butter market in this country. When Canadian organizations commenced cutting the price of butter to a point that we thought was nearly rock bottom, I agreed that the Australians could release their butter at a price less than thirty-two cents a pound.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In other words, the minister
admits he has nothing to do with naming the price of butter in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So long as the production
of butter in this country is less than the consumption, is it necessary, in order to supply the trade and the public in general, to import butter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Do I understand
the hon. member's question to be this: If the production of butter in Canada is less than the consumption, should we allow the importation of butter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; is it necessary to
import butter from outside?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have just a word to
say on this subject. During the last campaign the butter question was very much under discussion in every county in Quebec. I held several joint meetings and at some in particular the perpetual Tory candidate in my constituency said that in Australia and New Zealand they had great opportunities that were denied to Canada. I think he said that in New Zealand in one year they had 100,000 cows and the year after they had 1,200,000. I said: Those are not cows; they are rabbits. At that time that gentleman was blaming the previous administration for having permitted the importation of butter from the other dominions. If my memory serves me aright, the Liberal party was blamed some years ago by the hon. member for East Kootenay, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, for not being agreeable enough to Australia and New Zealand. During the campaign, Conservative speakers made 
this statement-and this is important because many people voted Conservative on account of it-that if the present Prime Minister came into power, not a pound of butter from New Zealand or Australia would be admitted into Canada. This was stated on the hustings everywhere in my constituency, and I am surprised to see that some butter is being imported by Canada at this time. The question was fair, and it has been answered very fairly not only by the Minister of Agriculture, with whom I sympathize very much at the present time, but also, I think, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who evidently said yes when I asked the question about the importation of butter being necessary because the production is much less than the consumption at this time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No one takes the hon.
member seriously.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Halifax is not in the butter business; he is not elected by farmers. He is in the soft drink business. He knows nothing about the matter except that he may put some butter in his soft drinks. I come from a farming constituency. I am interested in the production of butter and I took the trouble to study the matter in order to see what can be done for our people.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was people like the hon.
member who defeated their own party.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Liberal party was
defeated by a trick. Last year when the Liberal government was in power, butter was much dearer than it is now. What was said to the electors of this country during the last campaign was this:	If you elect the Conservatives, the price of butter will be forty cents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Seventy cents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They said: At least forty cents. It was a minimum and it could have gone up to ninety-nine cents, to be less than a dollar. But they told the farmers: if you elect the Conservatives; if you elect the right hon. member, who is now the Prime Minister of this country, the price of butter will rise from thirty-two cents to forty cents, but it has fallen from thirty-two cents to seventeen cents a pound.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fourteen cents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When it is sold at 17 cents, it means that the farmer here is left with only 14 cents a pound, and that is the marvellous result that was to be brought about as soon as the Conservative party got into power.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
This is a thing that will be reported in Hansard to-morrow, and the people will read it. The Conservative party promised in every constituency in this country to bring about this wonderful result. This shows what fakers can say to the people of this country. They go to the limit. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Quinn) is not smiling now. He reminds me of someone with an enamelled face who is afraid to smile for fear it will crack the enamel and the crack will show.
During the last election the farmers of this country were deceived by the Conservative party, and not only that but every Conservative speaker went on the platform and said that the Liberal party was working against the best interests of the farming class. Yet at that time, Mr. Chairman, butter sold at more than 30 cents a pound, and now it is less than 17 cents. Are my hon. friends opposite satisfied with that progress? What are they going to do about it? They pretended that a tariff was going to help the fanner. They said: Let us put a duty on butter that comes in from abroad, and you will see butter prices go up.
I have something here, Mr. Chairman, that I keep for special occasions, and I shall use it now. It is nothing harmful-the question of ammunition was settled yesterday afternoon. It is the opinion of a man whom my hon. friend (Mr. Quinn) supported and banged bis desk for with great violence every time he rose to address the house. He does not know yet of whom I am speaking. I am speaking of a gentleman, who, though he might be in the shade to-night, will one day come into the limelight as leader of the opposition after the Conservative party is defeated in the next election. I mean the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. In view of the disastrous incompetence that has been shown by this government since it came into power, I know Very well that my hon. friends of the opposition, who can scream now, say in private that they are very sorry that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen is not now in this house;
I.	would not say now as the leader of the party, but as the right hand of the leader. On April 8, 1926-more than five years ago-how times have changed since then!-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were not here then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh yes, I was, and I shall be here for a long time. Since that time the Conservative convention took place, and after that convention my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) said that the Conservative party had been too honest in the
past. Here I have just a word to show that honesty is the best policy. The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen on April 8, 1926, was asked this question by Mr. Ross, then member for Moose Jaw:
You contend that if the tariff is taken off, prices immediately rise?
Note this, Mr. Chairman. This is' what a good friend of yours said, and at the time he was speaking from the bottom of his heart, with absolute honesty. I will repeat the question again for those who are willingly blind and deaf. Mr. Ross asked:
You contend that if the tariff is taken off, prices immediately rise?
And the man who has more brains in his head than anyone on the other side of the house replied:
We contend it, and we know it because we see the facts.
It was a forecast of what is happening today. Never was the duty so high on butter and never was the price so low. It seems as if this government was raising the tariff in order to give the manufacturers a chance to deprive the farmers of their legitimate profits.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More solemnity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is no tariff on birds. When my hon. friend the member for South Essex was bom he was attended by a nurse, and as soon as he came into this world she said. "He eccles," and that name was given to him.
Here we have a most serious arraignment of this government, Mr, Chairman, coming from the lips of the man who was the leader of the Conservative party for a long time, and who since that time has not been eclipsed by anyone on the opposite side. He said: We contend that if the tariff is taken off, the' prices immediately rise, and we know it because we see the facts. A high tariff has been imposed on butter and on potatoes. My hon. friend from Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Smith) and his. colleague from New Brunswick know all about potatoes; they could sing a hymn to potatoes. There was an ancient writer who said: "O virtue, what crimes are committed in thy name!" I would say to my hon. friend from New Brunswick: "0 potato, what crimes are committed in thy name!"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To come back to butter,
Mr. Chairman, and speaking at the same time of potatoes, we have on the opposite side of the house some supermen, or semi-gods, who told the electorate: We cure everything; we will make you farmers happy; we will allow
Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

you industrialists to profiteer more than you ever did before in your lives; you labouring men will get better wages than you ever got before, and you will get work; the ^ons of the farmers will get nice positions and everyone will be happy. How was it to be done? I will not say that everyone was to have a soft drink, because that would not be very tempting, but, Mr. Chairman, I do say that the people were badly deceived during the last campaign by that cry of high tariff.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order. I would ask
hon. gentlemen not to make so much noise. They have at least the privilege to go out, which I have not, so I would ask them to keep order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The tariff was to be a cure for every disease. It was to make people happy. Everybody was to be as happy as a man who is in heaven as soon as that new tariff was applied. It has been applied, and applied with great vigour; for I will say this for hon. gentlemen opposite, that they have been consistent. They proposed to increase the tariff, and they have done so. What has been the result? The result has been that farm products are to-day selling for nothing. I am sorry for the farmers of this country who are suffering more than ever before because of the unfair prices they are receiving for their products. The small prices received for farm produce represents a great menace for the future, because the farmers may not cultivate their lands with so much care or to such an extent if they do not receive a reasonable profit from their labours.
The situation is worse than ever. I do not wish to criticize the present Minister of Agriculture, who I admit is trying to do his best for the welfare of the farmers of Canada. I wish however to tell him that the policy of high tariff is a fake, it is a mirage, something which will give nothing to the farmer but which will contribute to the enrichment of a few. It will not profit the farmer but it will make wealthy those who control the trusts, the great organizations. It will not make the poor man rich but will make the rich man still richer, and the wealth of the nation will be no better distributed than it is now.
May I ask the Minister of Agriculture seriously to consider the effect of tariff on farm products? I have before me a statement of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen to the effect that "as soon as the tariff is off the prices rise." On the other hand, the tariff
on farm products has been raised and prices have since declined. This statement would show that Right Hon. Arthur Meighen knew more about economics than hon. members now sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: It is moved by the Hon. Mr. Guthrie, seconded by Hon. Mr. Stevens, that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

Progress reported.
